docs.text: duckdb-zarr ¶ A DuckDB extension for querying Zarr-format scientific arrays with SQL. Read How it works for the array-to-table model and SQL reference. What It Does ¶ duckdb-zarr extends DuckDB with the ability to query Zarr arrays directly using SQL. Zarr is a format for storing chunked, compressed N-dimensional arrays, widely used in scientific computing and big data applications—particularly in climate science, astronomy, genomics, and remote sensing. With this extension, you can: Query Zarr array metadata (dimensions, chunk structure, data type, attributes) Read array data directly into DuckDB tables Combine Zarr data with other data sources using standard SQL joins The Pivot Concept ¶ Zarr arrays are n-dimensional gridded data (like satellite imagery, climate model outputs, or sensor readings). This extension "pivots" these multi-dimensional arrays into relational tables—treating each cell in the array as a row, with coordinates as columns. This lets you use familiar SQL to query data that would otherwise require specialized array-processing tools. Thinking in arrays and SQL ¶ The array-to-table approach explored by xarray-sql provides a useful way to think about these queries: Coordinates become columns: a dense array has one row per coordinate combination, with measurements as value columns. WHERE selects a region: filter by time, location, channel, or depth. GROUP BY chooses the dimensions you keep: grouping by latitude and longitude while averaging a measurement reduces over time. Compatible variables share a table: variables with matching dimensions and shape in one Zarr group can be queried together. Join separate tables explicitly. For example, average air temperature over the selected year at each location. After loading the extension, run this from the repository root with the tutorial fixtures generated ( make generate_fixtures ): SELECT lat, lon, AVG(air) AS mean_air FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/air_temperature.zarr') WHERE time >= TIMESTAMP '2014-01-01' AND time < TIMESTAMP '2015-01-01' GROUP BY lat, lon; These are shared principles, not an xarray-sql API compatibility layer: duckdb-zarr reads Zarr directly inside DuckDB, without a Python layer. Sparse AnnData tables can contain only stored entries rather than every coordinate combination. A WHERE filter does not by itself guarantee that chunks are skipped. Why This Is Useful ¶ Scientific datasets are often stored in Zarr format because it handles multi-terabyte to petabyte-scale arrays efficiently through chunking and compression. However, traditional SQL databases don't understand Zarr. This extension bridges that gap—allowing data scientists and engineers to: Query Zarr metadata without loading entire arrays into memory Perform SQL analytics on scientific data alongside structured data Use DuckDB's fast SQL engine to filter and aggregate chunked array data Integrate Zarr data pipelines with existing SQL-based workflows This project is related to xarray-sql and zarr-datafusion , which offer related SQL interfaces to scientific arrays. Field guides ¶ Biology — interactive single-cell and 3D image queries. Climate — temperature summaries and precipitation. Geoscience — Landsat composites and vegetation indices. Guides by domain ¶ Biology: AnnData annotated matrices , with a cell-by-gene example and a section on AnnData tables in SpatialData stores; OME-Zarr bioimages . Try the single-page duckdb-zarr for biologists browser example : editable SQL over a real single-cell RNA-seq UMAP and a rotatable 3D fluorescence volume, both backed by a Zarr-URL box you can repoint at your own S3/HTTPS store. Climate and geoscience: gridded-data quick start below; tested atmospheric and ocean datasets . General reference: How duckdb-zarr works , including how arrays become tables , the SQL interface , known limits , and roadmap ; tested scientific domains . Quick Start ¶ Installation ¶ Pre-built binaries : not published yet. Build from source (see Development Setup below) Basic Usage ¶ -- Load the extension LOAD 'zarr'; -- Read metadata from a Zarr store (a local path or a URL) SELECT * FROM read_zarr_metadata('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/float_baseline.zarr'); -- Read a store as a table SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/float_baseline.zarr'); -- Filter with plain SQL on the coordinate columns, dates included SELECT time, lat, lon, air FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/air_temperature.zarr') WHERE lat > 0 AND time >= TIMESTAMP '2014-06-01'; Time coordinates stored the CF way — a number plus a units attr like "hours since 1800-01-01" — are decoded to TIMESTAMP , which is why the query above can compare time against a date literal. Pass decode_times := false if you want the raw on-disk offsets instead. For a small bioimage walkthrough, see Querying OME-Zarr . For annotated matrices written by AnnData, see Querying AnnData stores . For the domains covered by the current test suite, see Tested scientific domains . Nested groups and DataTree stores ¶ A nested store has one set of tables per Zarr group. read_zarr(store) reads only the root group; it does not combine sibling groups, even when their arrays have identical names, dimensions and shapes. This is a change from older releases, which pooled arrays across the store. Discover the tables first, then select a group and its table: SELECT group_path, schema_name, table_name, dims, data_vars FROM read_zarr_tables('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/datatree.zarr') ORDER BY group_path; SELECT x, y, foo FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/datatree.zarr', group_path := 'simulation/fine', table_name := 'x_y') ORDER BY x, y; Coordinates are inherited from ancestor groups, so the second query uses the root's x values. Misaligned groups have a NULL table_name in the catalog and cannot be read as a table. dims := ['x', 'y'] is an alternative to table_name := 'x_y' ; do not pass both. Catalog columns such as dims and data_vars are SQL lists, not JSON strings. read_zarr_groups remains an alias of read_zarr_tables . For arrays without dimension names, select one explicitly with array_path := . Its unnamed axes become integer-position columns dim_0 , dim_1 , and so on, or pass dims := to label those positions yourself for this query. Group tables omit these arrays rather than joining unrelated data by position. AnnData has its own axis naming and decoded tables; see the AnnData guide . See arrays without dimension names for the full dims := rules. To mount all readable tables as views, call read_zarr_views(store, database) and execute the returned SQL statements on the same connection. It returns SQL; it does not execute the statements itself. See the Python and CLI mounting recipes . OME-Zarr Features ¶ OME-Zarr stores often contain nested arrays for resolution levels and labels. Use metadata discovery first to see the available store-relative paths: SELECT name, dims, shape, dtype FROM read_zarr_metadata('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr'); Then pass array_path= when you want a specific image or label array: SELECT c, AVG(value) AS mean_intensity FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr', array_path='0') GROUP BY c; SELECT value AS label, COUNT(*) AS pixels FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr', array_path='labels/nuclei/0') WHERE value > 0 GROUP BY label; array_path is optional for simple stores where the reader can infer a single compatible array group. It becomes useful for multiscale images, nested labels, or stores with multiple incompatible array shapes. docs.text: Querying AnnData stores ¶ AnnData is a file format of the scverse ecosystem for annotated data matrices. Its axes are observations ( obs ) and variables ( var ), not necessarily cells and genes. This page uses a cell-by-gene example to query a store that AnnData.write_zarr() wrote: annotations ( obs , var ), the expression matrix ( X ), layers , embeddings ( obsm ) and pairwise matrices ( obsp , varp ). The examples use the small test store in this repository. Run make generate_fixtures to create it. The store has 20 cells, named cell_0 to cell_19 , and 8 genes, named gene_0 to gene_7 . When to use SQL instead of loading an AnnData object ¶ Use anndata.read_zarr when you want an AnnData object for slicing, analysis, or plotting in Python. Use duckdb-zarr when the result you need is a table: counts by annotation, expression summaries, or joins to sample metadata in CSV, Parquet, or another DuckDB table. You can query the store from SQL without first constructing an AnnData object. This is a relational view of the data, not a replacement for AnnData's analysis APIs or a full round-trip representation of the object. Start with read_zarr_tables to discover the available tables. Use read_zarr with table_name := and, for child groups, group_path := for a one-off query. It decodes annotations and uses observation and variable names as coordinates, so you can join obs , var , and X by name. Use read_zarr_views when several queries should share stable table names. Run the returned SQL to create views; the views still read the Zarr store, rather than copying it into DuckDB. Use array_path := for a single array or encoded element, including arrays under uns , or to inspect encoding components. This lower-level route uses integer positions instead of observation and variable names; prefer the tables for annotation joins. Sparse tables omit unstored zeros, so SQL aggregates need care: see Sparse matrices omit zeros . See Limits before substituting SQL reads for an AnnData workflow. How a store maps to tables ¶ The extension reads an AnnData store as a tree of tables. Each Zarr group is a DuckDB schema, and each set of variables with the same dimensions in a group is one table. The root group is the schema main . The design is in docs/design.md , decisions 8 and 9. Element Dimensions Table X obs , var main.obs_var obs columns obs main.obs var columns var main.var layers/* obs , var layers.obs_var obsm/<k> obs , <k>_component obsm.obs_<k>_component varm/<k> var , <k>_component varm.var_<k>_component obsp/* obs_i , obs_j obsp.obs_i_obs_j varp/* var_i , var_j varp.var_i_var_j raw/X obs , raw_var raw.obs_raw_var raw/var columns raw_var raw.raw_var The obs column holds the cell name ( obs_names in AnnData) and the var column holds the gene name ( var_names ). Every table has these names, so you can filter and join any table by name. Both axes of obsp show cell names, and both axes of varp show gene names. The <k>_component column of an obsm table is the component number, from 0. If a data frame has a column with the same name as its axis, for example an obs column called obs , that column keeps its path in the store as its name, "obs/obs" . Otherwise it would have the same name as the column of cell names. The extension decodes AnnData's encodings: A categorical column with string categories reads as a DuckDB ENUM of its categories. A categorical with other categories (for example integers) reads as the type of its categories. A missing value is NULL . A nullable column ( nullable-integer , nullable-boolean , nullable-string-array ) reads as its values, with NULL where the mask is set. A sparse matrix ( csr_matrix or csc_matrix ) reads as one row for each stored entry. See Sparse matrices omit zeros . The extension does not read uns . Read its arrays one at a time with array_path= (see Read one array ). List the tables ¶ read_zarr_tables gives one row for each table. group_path is the Zarr group, schema_name is the DuckDB schema for that group, and table_name is the table name. SELECT group_path, schema_name, table_name, dims FROM read_zarr_tables('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr'); / main obs [obs] / main obs_var [obs, var] / main var [var] /layers layers obs_var [obs, var] /obsm obsm obs_X_umap_component [obs, X_umap_component] /obsp obsp obs_i_obs_j [obs_i, obs_j] /varp varp var_i_var_j [var_i, var_j] Read a table ¶ read_zarr reads the root group. The root has three tables, so use table_name := to select one by the name read_zarr_tables gives it ( dims := with its dimensions works too). Use group_path := to read another group. -- Cell annotations: one row for each cell SELECT obs, cell_type, donor, n_genes FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs'); -- Gene annotations: one row for each gene SELECT var, gene_symbol, mean_expr FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'var'); -- The expression matrix: one row for each stored entry SELECT obs, var, X FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs_var'); -- Two layers of one cell, by name SELECT var, spliced, unspliced FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'layers') WHERE obs = 'cell_0'; In this store, cell_4 has no cell type, so cell_type is NULL for cell_4 . gene_6 has no symbol, so gene_symbol is NULL for gene_6 . "group" := is the same parameter as group_path := . GROUP is a keyword in DuckDB, so the quotes are necessary. Mount the store as a database ¶ Views give each table a stable name, so queries do not repeat read_zarr . read_zarr_views returns the SQL statements that mount the store, one statement in each row. Run the statements in order and stop on the first error. They attach a new in-memory database, create one schema for each group, and create one view for each table. The database alias must not already exist; the first statement rejects it rather than replacing its views. SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc'); ATTACH ':memory:' AS "pbmc"; CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."obs" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs'); CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."obs_var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs_var'); CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'var'); CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "pbmc"."layers"; CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."layers"."obs_var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'layers', table_name := 'obs_var'); ... In Python, run each row: for (sql,) in con.sql("SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc')").fetchall(): con.execute(sql) In the DuckDB CLI, write the rows to a file, then read the file: .bail on .mode list .headers off .once mount.sql SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc'); .read mount.sql A table in main needs no schema name: pbmc.obs is pbmc.main.obs . The examples in the rest of this page use these views. To give a view a different name, use view_names := . A key is a table name from read_zarr_tables . For a table that is not in the root group, the key starts with the group path: SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc', view_names := MAP {'obs_var': 'X', 'layers/obs_var': 'layers'}); The views read the store again for each query. If you run many queries, CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies the data into DuckDB once. Sparse matrices omit zeros ¶ AnnData usually stores X as a sparse matrix. A table of sparse matrices has a row only where a matrix stores a value. A missing row means the value is 0. This store has 27 stored entries in a matrix of 160 cells, so the X table has 27 rows. A matrix can store one position more than once if it was written without scipy's sum_duplicates() . That position gives one row, with the sum of the entries, as in scipy and anndata. For this reason, AVG(X) over the X table is a mean over the stored entries only. To get a mean over cells, start from obs and use a LEFT JOIN . Each cell then has one row, and COALESCE gives 0 to the cells that have no entry: -- Mean expression of Cd4 in each cell type SELECT o.cell_type, AVG(COALESCE(x.X, 0)) AS mean_cd4 FROM pbmc.obs o LEFT JOIN ( SELECT x.obs, x.X FROM pbmc.obs_var x JOIN pbmc.var v USING (var) WHERE v.gene_symbol = 'Cd4' ) x USING (obs) GROUP BY o.cell_type; B cell 17.666667 NK cell 9.333333 T cell 23.142857 NULL 0.000000 When the gene names are the gene symbols, the inner query is not necessary: LEFT JOIN pbmc.obs_var x ON x.obs = o.obs AND x.var = 'CD4' . If a group has two or more sparse matrices with the same dimensions, they share one table. The table has a row for each position that at least one matrix stores. A matrix that has no value at that position reads as 0 in that row. In this store, layers/spliced stores 53 entries and layers/unspliced stores 80. The layers.obs_var table has 106 rows, because 27 positions are in both. If a group has a sparse matrix and a dense array with the same dimensions, the table has a row for each cell. The sparse matrix reads as 0 where it stores no value. In this store, varp has a dense corr and a sparse corr_csc , so the varp.var_i_var_j table has 64 rows. Embeddings and pairwise matrices ¶ An obsm table has one row for each cell and component. Use FILTER or PIVOT to get one column for each component: -- UMAP coordinates of each cell SELECT u.obs, MAX(u.X_umap) FILTER (WHERE u.X_umap_component = 0) AS umap_1, MAX(u.X_umap) FILTER (WHERE u.X_umap_component = 1) AS umap_2 FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'obsm') u GROUP BY u.obs; An obsp table has one row for each stored pair of cells. For a neighbor graph, the neighbors of one cell are: SELECT obs_j AS neighbor, connectivities FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'obsp') WHERE obs_i = 'cell_3'; Cell names must be unique ¶ Joins on obs and var compare names. If two cells have the same name, a join matches each row of one cell to both cells, and the result has extra rows. anndata warns about duplicate names when it loads such a store. Make the names unique before you write the store, for example with adata.obs_names_make_unique() and adata.var_names_make_unique() . Read one array ¶ array_path := reads one array and ignores the group structure. Use it for uns , or to look at the arrays that hold an encoded column. An AnnData element gets the same dimension names as in its table, but one array has no index to take names from, so its dimension columns hold integer positions. For example, array_path := 'obs/n_genes' gives the columns obs (0 to 19) and value . An array inside an encoded group has no AnnData dimensions. Its dimensions are dim_0 , dim_1 , and so on. For example, array_path := 'obs/cell_type/codes' gives the integer codes in the columns dim_0 and value , and the categories are not applied. Pass dims := to replace that placeholder with a more useful name for this query: SELECT cell, value FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', array_path := 'obs/cell_type/codes', dims := ['cell']) ORDER BY cell; The value is still the raw category code; it does not become a coordinate, and dims := cannot rename the already-named obs / var dimensions of an ordinary AnnData table read. See How duckdb-zarr works for the full rules. read_zarr_metadata lists every array. The array_path_dims column gives the dimension names that array_path := uses for each array. With group_path := , it lists the arrays of that group's tables: group_path := '/' gives the arrays of X and of the obs and var columns. SELECT name, dtype, shape, array_path_dims FROM read_zarr_metadata('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr') ORDER BY name; array_path := also selects an encoded column on its own, decoded: a sparse matrix, a categorical or a nullable column. Like one array, its dimension columns hold integer positions. For example, array_path := 'X' gives the stored entries of a sparse X as obs , var and value , and read_zarr_metadata(store, array_path := 'X') lists the arrays it is made of. group_path := cannot name an encoded column, because it is not a group of tables. SpatialData stores ¶ This section covers the AnnData tables inside SpatialData stores and a join to a label image. It is not a comprehensive SpatialData tutorial and does not cover coordinate transformations or spatial analysis APIs. The tested example uses a small synthetic SpatialData-like store; it does not validate every SpatialData element or storage version. A SpatialData store keeps each table as an AnnData object at tables/<name> . The extension reads any group with encoding-type: anndata as an AnnData object, so each table is a schema of its own: tables/cells has the tables obs , var and obs_var , and tables/cells/obsm has the embeddings, with the cell names of tables/cells . The other elements of a SpatialData store are not AnnData: Element Format Read it with images/<name> , labels/<name> OME-Zarr read_zarr . Read one scale with array_path := 'labels/<name>/s0' . points/<name> Parquet files in points.parquet/ read_parquet('store.zarr/points/<name>/points.parquet/*.parquet') shapes/<name> GeoParquet file shapes.parquet read_parquet('store.zarr/shapes/<name>/shapes.parquet') . The geometry column is a DuckDB GEOMETRY . tables/<name> AnnData read_zarr with group_path := 'tables/<name>' A table's attributes name the element it annotates ( region ), the obs column that holds that element's name ( region_key ), and the obs column that holds the instance id ( instance_key ). Join the table to the element on the instance id: In a label image, the pixel value is the instance id. In points, the instance id is a column, usually instance_id . In shapes, the instance id is the row's index. GeoPandas does not write a default index (0, 1, 2, ...), so use the row number: read_parquet(..., file_row_number := true) adds it as file_row_number . The example store test/fixtures/anndata/spatialdata_like.zarr has a label image labels/cells and a table tables/cells that annotates it. This query gives the area in pixels of each cell: SELECT o.instance_id, o.region, COUNT(*) AS area_px FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/spatialdata_like.zarr', array_path := 'labels/cells/s0') AS l JOIN read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/spatialdata_like.zarr', group_path := 'tables/cells', table_name := 'obs') AS o ON l.value = o.instance_id GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY area_px DESC; ┌─────────────┬────────┬─────────┐ │ instance_id │ region │ area_px │ ├─────────────┼────────┼─────────┤ │ 2 │ cells │ 4 │ │ 1 │ cells │ 3 │ │ 3 │ cells │ 2 │ └─────────────┴────────┴─────────┘ read_zarr_views mounts the tables and labels of a SpatialData store, for example as sd."tables/cells".obs . It does not mount points or shapes, because they are not Zarr. Create views for them with read_parquet . Limits ¶ The extension uses this layout only in groups with encoding-type: anndata . An old store that has no encoding-type attributes reads only with array_path := . The extension does not read uns or awkward arrays. In a MuData store, the modalities ( mod/<name> ) read as AnnData objects, but the global obs and var do not. Sparse matrices with the same dimensions and no dense array beside them share a table only if all are CSR or all are CSC. A table that mixes the two has no table_name in read_zarr_tables ; read each matrix with array_path := . If two columns of one data frame differ only in case, or one has the name of its axis, they keep their paths as names ( "obs/obs" ), because DuckDB column names ignore case. A path that still collides gets a number ( "obs/Obs_1" ). Remote stores need consolidated metadata to list arrays. Without it, only array_path := works.

docs.text: AnnData is a file format of the scverse ecosystem for annotated data matrices. Its axes are observations ( obs ) and variables ( var ), not necessarily cells and genes. This page uses a cell-by-gene example to query a store that AnnData.write_zarr() wrote: annotations ( obs , var ), the expression matrix ( X ), layers , embeddings ( obsm ) and pairwise matrices ( obsp , varp ). The examples use the small test store in this repository. Run make generate_fixtures to create it. The store has 20 cells, named cell_0 to cell_19 , and 8 genes, named gene_0 to gene_7 .
docs.title: Querying AnnData stores

docs.text: Use anndata.read_zarr when you want an AnnData object for slicing, analysis, or plotting in Python. Use duckdb-zarr when the result you need is a table: counts by annotation, expression summaries, or joins to sample metadata in CSV, Parquet, or another DuckDB table. You can query the store from SQL without first constructing an AnnData object. This is a relational view of the data, not a replacement for AnnData's analysis APIs or a full round-trip representation of the object. Start with read_zarr_tables to discover the available tables. Use read_zarr with table_name := and, for child groups, group_path := for a one-off query. It decodes annotations and uses observation and variable names as coordinates, so you can join obs , var , and X by name. Use read_zarr_views when several queries should share stable table names. Run the returned SQL to create views; the views still read the Zarr store, rather than copying it into DuckDB. Use array_path := for a single array or encoded element, including arrays under uns , or to inspect encoding components. This lower-level route uses integer positions instead of observation and variable names; prefer the tables for annotation joins. Sparse tables omit unstored zeros, so SQL aggregates need care: see Sparse matrices omit zeros . See Limits before substituting SQL reads for an AnnData workflow.
docs.title: When to use SQL instead of loading an AnnData object

docs.text: The extension reads an AnnData store as a tree of tables. Each Zarr group is a DuckDB schema, and each set of variables with the same dimensions in a group is one table. The root group is the schema main . The design is in docs/design.md , decisions 8 and 9. Element Dimensions Table X obs , var main.obs_var obs columns obs main.obs var columns var main.var layers/* obs , var layers.obs_var obsm/<k> obs , <k>_component obsm.obs_<k>_component varm/<k> var , <k>_component varm.var_<k>_component obsp/* obs_i , obs_j obsp.obs_i_obs_j varp/* var_i , var_j varp.var_i_var_j raw/X obs , raw_var raw.obs_raw_var raw/var columns raw_var raw.raw_var The obs column holds the cell name ( obs_names in AnnData) and the var column holds the gene name ( var_names ). Every table has these names, so you can filter and join any table by name. Both axes of obsp show cell names, and both axes of varp show gene names. The <k>_component column of an obsm table is the component number, from 0. If a data frame has a column with the same name as its axis, for example an obs column called obs , that column keeps its path in the store as its name, "obs/obs" . Otherwise it would have the same name as the column of cell names. The extension decodes AnnData's encodings: A categorical column with string categories reads as a DuckDB ENUM of its categories. A categorical with other categories (for example integers) reads as the type of its categories. A missing value is NULL . A nullable column ( nullable-integer , nullable-boolean , nullable-string-array ) reads as its values, with NULL where the mask is set. A sparse matrix ( csr_matrix or csc_matrix ) reads as one row for each stored entry. See Sparse matrices omit zeros . The extension does not read uns . Read its arrays one at a time with array_path= (see Read one array ).
docs.title: How a store maps to tables

docs.text: read_zarr_tables gives one row for each table. group_path is the Zarr group, schema_name is the DuckDB schema for that group, and table_name is the table name. SELECT group_path, schema_name, table_name, dims FROM read_zarr_tables('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr'); / main obs [obs] / main obs_var [obs, var] / main var [var] /layers layers obs_var [obs, var] /obsm obsm obs_X_umap_component [obs, X_umap_component] /obsp obsp obs_i_obs_j [obs_i, obs_j] /varp varp var_i_var_j [var_i, var_j]
docs.title: List the tables

docs.text: read_zarr reads the root group. The root has three tables, so use table_name := to select one by the name read_zarr_tables gives it ( dims := with its dimensions works too). Use group_path := to read another group. -- Cell annotations: one row for each cell SELECT obs, cell_type, donor, n_genes FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs'); -- Gene annotations: one row for each gene SELECT var, gene_symbol, mean_expr FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'var'); -- The expression matrix: one row for each stored entry SELECT obs, var, X FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs_var'); -- Two layers of one cell, by name SELECT var, spliced, unspliced FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'layers') WHERE obs = 'cell_0'; In this store, cell_4 has no cell type, so cell_type is NULL for cell_4 . gene_6 has no symbol, so gene_symbol is NULL for gene_6 . "group" := is the same parameter as group_path := . GROUP is a keyword in DuckDB, so the quotes are necessary.
docs.title: Read a table

docs.text: Views give each table a stable name, so queries do not repeat read_zarr . read_zarr_views returns the SQL statements that mount the store, one statement in each row. Run the statements in order and stop on the first error. They attach a new in-memory database, create one schema for each group, and create one view for each table. The database alias must not already exist; the first statement rejects it rather than replacing its views. SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc'); ATTACH ':memory:' AS "pbmc"; CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."obs" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs'); CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."obs_var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'obs_var'); CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."main"."var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', table_name := 'var'); CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "pbmc"."layers"; CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "pbmc"."layers"."obs_var" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'layers', table_name := 'obs_var'); ... In Python, run each row: for (sql,) in con.sql("SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc')").fetchall(): con.execute(sql) In the DuckDB CLI, write the rows to a file, then read the file: .bail on .mode list .headers off .once mount.sql SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc'); .read mount.sql A table in main needs no schema name: pbmc.obs is pbmc.main.obs . The examples in the rest of this page use these views. To give a view a different name, use view_names := . A key is a table name from read_zarr_tables . For a table that is not in the root group, the key starts with the group path: SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('pbmc_like.zarr', 'pbmc', view_names := MAP {'obs_var': 'X', 'layers/obs_var': 'layers'}); The views read the store again for each query. If you run many queries, CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT copies the data into DuckDB once.
docs.title: Mount the store as a database

docs.text: AnnData usually stores X as a sparse matrix. A table of sparse matrices has a row only where a matrix stores a value. A missing row means the value is 0. This store has 27 stored entries in a matrix of 160 cells, so the X table has 27 rows. A matrix can store one position more than once if it was written without scipy's sum_duplicates() . That position gives one row, with the sum of the entries, as in scipy and anndata. For this reason, AVG(X) over the X table is a mean over the stored entries only. To get a mean over cells, start from obs and use a LEFT JOIN . Each cell then has one row, and COALESCE gives 0 to the cells that have no entry: -- Mean expression of Cd4 in each cell type SELECT o.cell_type, AVG(COALESCE(x.X, 0)) AS mean_cd4 FROM pbmc.obs o LEFT JOIN ( SELECT x.obs, x.X FROM pbmc.obs_var x JOIN pbmc.var v USING (var) WHERE v.gene_symbol = 'Cd4' ) x USING (obs) GROUP BY o.cell_type; B cell 17.666667 NK cell 9.333333 T cell 23.142857 NULL 0.000000 When the gene names are the gene symbols, the inner query is not necessary: LEFT JOIN pbmc.obs_var x ON x.obs = o.obs AND x.var = 'CD4' . If a group has two or more sparse matrices with the same dimensions, they share one table. The table has a row for each position that at least one matrix stores. A matrix that has no value at that position reads as 0 in that row. In this store, layers/spliced stores 53 entries and layers/unspliced stores 80. The layers.obs_var table has 106 rows, because 27 positions are in both. If a group has a sparse matrix and a dense array with the same dimensions, the table has a row for each cell. The sparse matrix reads as 0 where it stores no value. In this store, varp has a dense corr and a sparse corr_csc , so the varp.var_i_var_j table has 64 rows.
docs.title: Sparse matrices omit zeros

docs.text: An obsm table has one row for each cell and component. Use FILTER or PIVOT to get one column for each component: -- UMAP coordinates of each cell SELECT u.obs, MAX(u.X_umap) FILTER (WHERE u.X_umap_component = 0) AS umap_1, MAX(u.X_umap) FILTER (WHERE u.X_umap_component = 1) AS umap_2 FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'obsm') u GROUP BY u.obs; An obsp table has one row for each stored pair of cells. For a neighbor graph, the neighbors of one cell are: SELECT obs_j AS neighbor, connectivities FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', group_path := 'obsp') WHERE obs_i = 'cell_3';
docs.title: Embeddings and pairwise matrices

docs.text: Joins on obs and var compare names. If two cells have the same name, a join matches each row of one cell to both cells, and the result has extra rows. anndata warns about duplicate names when it loads such a store. Make the names unique before you write the store, for example with adata.obs_names_make_unique() and adata.var_names_make_unique() .
docs.title: Cell names must be unique

docs.text: array_path := reads one array and ignores the group structure. Use it for uns , or to look at the arrays that hold an encoded column. An AnnData element gets the same dimension names as in its table, but one array has no index to take names from, so its dimension columns hold integer positions. For example, array_path := 'obs/n_genes' gives the columns obs (0 to 19) and value . An array inside an encoded group has no AnnData dimensions. Its dimensions are dim_0 , dim_1 , and so on. For example, array_path := 'obs/cell_type/codes' gives the integer codes in the columns dim_0 and value , and the categories are not applied. Pass dims := to replace that placeholder with a more useful name for this query: SELECT cell, value FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr', array_path := 'obs/cell_type/codes', dims := ['cell']) ORDER BY cell; The value is still the raw category code; it does not become a coordinate, and dims := cannot rename the already-named obs / var dimensions of an ordinary AnnData table read. See How duckdb-zarr works for the full rules. read_zarr_metadata lists every array. The array_path_dims column gives the dimension names that array_path := uses for each array. With group_path := , it lists the arrays of that group's tables: group_path := '/' gives the arrays of X and of the obs and var columns. SELECT name, dtype, shape, array_path_dims FROM read_zarr_metadata('test/fixtures/anndata/pbmc_like.zarr') ORDER BY name; array_path := also selects an encoded column on its own, decoded: a sparse matrix, a categorical or a nullable column. Like one array, its dimension columns hold integer positions. For example, array_path := 'X' gives the stored entries of a sparse X as obs , var and value , and read_zarr_metadata(store, array_path := 'X') lists the arrays it is made of. group_path := cannot name an encoded column, because it is not a group of tables.
docs.title: Read one array

docs.text: This section covers the AnnData tables inside SpatialData stores and a join to a label image. It is not a comprehensive SpatialData tutorial and does not cover coordinate transformations or spatial analysis APIs. The tested example uses a small synthetic SpatialData-like store; it does not validate every SpatialData element or storage version. A SpatialData store keeps each table as an AnnData object at tables/<name> . The extension reads any group with encoding-type: anndata as an AnnData object, so each table is a schema of its own: tables/cells has the tables obs , var and obs_var , and tables/cells/obsm has the embeddings, with the cell names of tables/cells . The other elements of a SpatialData store are not AnnData: Element Format Read it with images/<name> , labels/<name> OME-Zarr read_zarr . Read one scale with array_path := 'labels/<name>/s0' . points/<name> Parquet files in points.parquet/ read_parquet('store.zarr/points/<name>/points.parquet/*.parquet') shapes/<name> GeoParquet file shapes.parquet read_parquet('store.zarr/shapes/<name>/shapes.parquet') . The geometry column is a DuckDB GEOMETRY . tables/<name> AnnData read_zarr with group_path := 'tables/<name>' A table's attributes name the element it annotates ( region ), the obs column that holds that element's name ( region_key ), and the obs column that holds the instance id ( instance_key ). Join the table to the element on the instance id: In a label image, the pixel value is the instance id. In points, the instance id is a column, usually instance_id . In shapes, the instance id is the row's index. GeoPandas does not write a default index (0, 1, 2, ...), so use the row number: read_parquet(..., file_row_number := true) adds it as file_row_number . It does not mount points or shapes, because they are not Zarr. Create views for them with read_parquet .

docs.text: Community Extension Release ¶ This project is set up to publish through DuckDB's community extension repository. DuckDB's process is descriptor-driven: submit a PR to duckdb/community-extensions with this repository's description.yml , and the community repository builds it with the same extension-ci-tools distribution workflow used here. Local Release Gate ¶ Run the local checks before opening the community PR: make release-check make test_release make release-check verifies the release-critical metadata that is easy to drift in a Rust C API extension: Makefile TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION Cargo.toml exact duckdb crate pin description.yml language , build , requires_toolchains , and excluded platforms Cargo.toml / pyproject.toml / description.yml development-placeholder versions agreeing with each other (see docs/versioning.md — this does not check them against any git tag; that sync happens automatically at release time) that MainDistributionPipeline.yml resolves duckdb_version from the Makefile pin at build time rather than carrying its own literal (see DuckDB Version Policy ) For the final community PR, also run: python3 scripts/check_release_ready.py --strict-community-ref That strict mode fails until description.yml repo.ref is an immutable release tag such as v0.1.0 or a 40-character commit hash. Do not submit ref: main . For release automation, leave the checked-in descriptor at ref: main and render the community descriptor for a tag: make render-community-descriptor REF=v0.1.0 The rendered file is written to build/community-extensions/extensions/zarr/description.yml with repo.ref set to the release tag. GitHub Release Automation ¶ Publishing a GitHub Release runs .github/workflows/community-release.yml . That workflow: Renders a community descriptor for the release tag. Validates the generated descriptor in strict mode. Uploads the descriptor as a workflow artifact. The workflow intentionally does not store or use a cross-repository token. A maintainer downloads the artifact and opens the PR to duckdb/community-extensions manually. This keeps release automation read-only inside this repository while still making the submitted descriptor reproducible. Running the workflow via Run workflow (workflow_dispatch) also accepts an optional ref_next input. Supply the commit built for the upcoming DuckDB version and it is emitted as repo.ref_next in the rendered descriptor — see Stable vs. Current DuckDB Main . Staying Current With DuckDB Releases ¶ The native adapter uses DuckDB's frozen v1.5.6 C API (see DuckDB Version Policy ). A version bump no longer necessarily requires a different binary, but every supported engine still needs build and query tests. Three pieces of automation support that process: CI guard — the Release metadata consistency job in .github/workflows/rust-quality.yml runs scripts/check_release_ready.py on every PR, so the DuckDB version pins can never merge out of sync. DuckDB Version Drift ( .github/workflows/duckdb-version-drift.yml ) runs daily . Within the current minor line it opens a chore/bump-duckdb-* PR as soon as pip duckdb and the matching duckdb crate publish a new patch. When a new minor or major DuckDB line appears (e.g. 1.5.x → 1.6.0 ) it opens a duckdb-major-bump tracking issue instead, because that is a manual migration (new CI-tools codename branch, possible source changes). ref_next lets you pre-stage the next line so there is no gap at all — covered below. The maintainer still cuts the release and opens the community PR (a deliberate choice — see above), but the source is kept release-ready automatically. Descriptor Notes ¶ The descriptor intentionally marks this as a Rust cargo extension and requests the extra toolchains that the community CI must install: extension: language: Rust build: cargo requires_toolchains: "rust;python3" The descriptor excludes only linux_amd64_musl . The local distribution workflow uses the same exclusion set. The wasm_mvp , wasm_eh , and wasm_threads platforms are built by CI (the wasm matrix has no test step — it builds and uploads artifacts only); re-add one to the exclusions if its build stops passing. Submission Steps ¶ Ensure main is green for Main Extension Distribution Pipeline and Rust quality . Update CHANGELOG.md (still manual). Do not bump Cargo.toml , pyproject.toml , or description.yml — they keep a development-placeholder version that scripts/sync_release_version.py syncs from the release tag automatically inside community-release.yml ; see docs/versioning.md . Create and publish a GitHub Release with a tag matching the project version, such as v0.1.0 . Download the validated descriptor artifact from the Community Extension Release workflow. Open a PR against duckdb/community-extensions adding or updating extensions/zarr/description.yml with that artifact. After the PR is merged and built by DuckDB's community infrastructure, users can install with: INSTALL zarr FROM community; LOAD zarr; DuckDB Version Policy ¶ DuckDB community extensions are distributed for DuckDB's latest stable release. This adapter sets USE_UNSTABLE_C_API=0 and DUCKDB_CAPI_VERSION=v1.5.6 . DuckDB 2.0 stabilized the formerly unstable v1 functions at that API version. The binary therefore advertises C_STRUCT with v1.5.6 metadata and exports zarr_init_c_api . Advertising C_STRUCT_UNSTABLE on DuckDB 2.0 instead selects the incompatible zarr_init_c_api_v2 entrypoint. TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION=v2.0.0 is the engine used by CI and Python tests, not the binary's API floor. The same native build has been tested on DuckDB 1.5.6 and 2.0.0. Older engines are below its declared API floor. Other engines and platforms need their own validation; accepting the metadata is not a query test. A target-engine bump must update these pins in one reviewed change: Makefile TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION Cargo.toml exact duckdb crate pin Cargo.lock The local release gate checks the first two and that the distribution pipeline resolves its duckdb_version from the Makefile. Cargo.lock should change when cargo update -p duckdb --precise <crate-version> is run. The distribution pipeline deliberately carries no duckdb_version: literal of its own: .github/workflows/MainDistributionPipeline.yml resolves it from TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION at build time. A literal inside a workflow file cannot be updated by an automated PR — GitHub refuses to let the Actions GITHUB_TOKEN push changes to files under .github/workflows/ under any permissions grant — so the drift bot's bump PRs would fail to push and the literal would silently go stale. One pin site, the Makefile, keeps the automated path working. The duckdb crate version encodes the engine's major, minor and patch numbers: v1.5.6 maps to 1.10506.0 , and the current v2.0.0 maps to: duckdb = { version = "=1.20000.0", features = ["loadable-extension"] } Do not bump DUCKDB_CAPI_VERSION with a routine engine update. It describes the API this adapter needs, not the installed engine. If that requirement changes, update the version requested in src/lib.rs and the compatibility tests too. Use the automated DuckDB Version Drift workflow for routine patch-line bumps. Treat major or minor DuckDB bumps as manual migrations: update the pins, rebuild, run make lint , and run make test_release before changing description.yml for community publication. Stable vs. Current DuckDB Main ¶ Near DuckDB releases, duckdb/community-extensions can test extensions against both the latest stable release and DuckDB main . If one commit cannot support both, maintain two refs: repo: github: xqlsystems/duckdb-zarr ref: <stable-compatible-tag-or-commit> ref_next: <duckdb-main-compatible-commit> Use ref for the commit that works with the latest stable DuckDB release. Use ref_next only when DuckDB main needs source changes that should not replace the stable build yet. After DuckDB releases, the community repository can promote the ref_next commit to ref . The current frozen-v1 adapter can use the same source and binary on the two validated engine versions. ref_next is only needed when a future engine needs source or ABI changes that cannot serve the current stable release. Validate both refs before publication; ref_next by itself does not establish support. Render a descriptor carrying both refs with: make render-community-descriptor REF=v0.1.1 REF_NEXT=<upcoming-commit-sha> REF_NEXT accepts a 40-character commit hash or a vX.Y.Z tag; the strict release check validates it is immutable. The rendered descriptor is written to build/community-extensions/extensions/zarr/description.yml . The community-release.yml workflow exposes the same ref_next as a dispatch input. Practical flow when a new DuckDB line is announced: Branch off main , apply the migration (CI-tools codename branch, version pins, any source fixes), and get CI green — this is the commit tracked by the duckdb-major-bump issue the drift bot opens. Submit a community PR whose descriptor sets ref to the current stable release and ref_next to that branch's HEAD commit. Once DuckDB releases, promote ref_next to ref on your next routine submission.

DuckDB Version Drift ( .github/workflows/duckdb-version-drift.yml ) runs daily . Within the current minor line it opens a chore/bump-duckdb-* PR as soon as pip duckdb and the matching duckdb crate publish a new patch. When a new minor or major DuckDB line appears (e.g. 1.5.x → 1.6.0 ) it opens a duckdb-major-bump tracking issue instead, because that is a manual migration (new CI-tools codename branch, possible source changes). ref_next lets you pre-stage the next line so there is no gap at all — covered below. The maintainer still cuts the release and opens the community PR (a deliberate choice — see above), but the source is kept release-ready automatically.
docs.title: Staying Current With DuckDB Releases

docs.text: The descriptor intentionally marks this as a Rust cargo extension and requests the extra toolchains that the community CI must install: extension: language: Rust build: cargo requires_toolchains: "rust;python3" The descriptor excludes only linux_amd64_musl . The local distribution workflow uses the same exclusion set. The wasm_mvp , wasm_eh , and wasm_threads platforms are built by CI (the wasm matrix has no test step — it builds and uploads artifacts only); re-add one to the exclusions if its build stops passing.
docs.title: Descriptor Notes

docs.text: Ensure main is green for Main Extension Distribution Pipeline and Rust quality . Update CHANGELOG.md (still manual). Do not bump Cargo.toml , pyproject.toml , or description.yml — they keep a development-placeholder version that scripts/sync_release_version.py syncs from the release tag automatically inside community-release.yml ; see docs/versioning.md . Create and publish a GitHub Release with a tag matching the project version, such as v0.1.0 . Download the validated descriptor artifact from the Community Extension Release workflow. Open a PR against duckdb/community-extensions adding or updating extensions/zarr/description.yml with that artifact. After the PR is merged and built by DuckDB's community infrastructure, users can install with: INSTALL zarr FROM community; LOAD zarr;
docs.title: Submission Steps

docs.text: DuckDB community extensions are distributed for DuckDB's latest stable release. This adapter sets USE_UNSTABLE_C_API=0 and DUCKDB_CAPI_VERSION=v1.5.6 . DuckDB 2.0 stabilized the formerly unstable v1 functions at that API version. The binary therefore advertises C_STRUCT with v1.5.6 metadata and exports zarr_init_c_api . Advertising C_STRUCT_UNSTABLE on DuckDB 2.0 instead selects the incompatible zarr_init_c_api_v2 entrypoint. TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION=v2.0.0 is the engine used by CI and Python tests, not the binary's API floor. The same native build has been tested on DuckDB 1.5.6 and 2.0.0. Older engines are below its declared API floor. Other engines and platforms need their own validation; accepting the metadata is not a query test. A target-engine bump must update these pins in one reviewed change: Makefile TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION Cargo.toml exact duckdb crate pin Cargo.lock The local release gate checks the first two and that the distribution pipeline resolves its duckdb_version from the Makefile. Cargo.lock should change when cargo update -p duckdb --precise <crate-version> is run. The distribution pipeline deliberately carries no duckdb_version: literal of its own: .github/workflows/MainDistributionPipeline.yml resolves it from TARGET_DUCKDB_VERSION at build time. A literal inside a workflow file cannot be updated by an automated PR — GitHub refuses to let the Actions GITHUB_TOKEN push changes to files under .github/workflows/ under any permissions grant — so the drift bot's bump PRs would fail to push and the literal would silently go stale. One pin site, the Makefile, keeps the automated path working. The duckdb crate version encodes the engine's major, minor and patch numbers: v1.5.6 maps to 1.10506.0 , and the current v2.0.0 maps to: duckdb = { version = "=1.20000.0", features = ["loadable-extension"] } Do not bump DUCKDB_CAPI_VERSION with a routine engine update. It describes the API this adapter needs, not the installed engine. If that requirement changes, update the version requested in src/lib.rs and the compatibility tests too. Use the automated DuckDB Version Drift workflow for routine patch-line bumps. Treat major or minor DuckDB bumps as manual migrations: update the pins, rebuild, run make lint , and run make test_release before changing description.yml for community publication.
docs.title: DuckDB Version Policy

docs.text: Near DuckDB releases, duckdb/community-extensions can test extensions against both the latest stable release and DuckDB main . If one commit cannot support both, maintain two refs: repo: github: xqlsystems/duckdb-zarr ref: <stable-compatible-tag-or-commit> ref_next: <duckdb-main-compatible-commit> Use ref for the commit that works with the latest stable DuckDB release. Use ref_next only when DuckDB main needs source changes that should not replace the stable build yet. After DuckDB releases, the community repository can promote the ref_next commit to ref . The current frozen-v1 adapter can use the same source and binary on the two validated engine versions. ref_next is only needed when a future engine needs source or ABI changes that cannot serve the current stable release. Validate both refs before publication; ref_next by itself does not establish support. Render a descriptor carrying both refs with: make render-community-descriptor REF=v0.1.1 REF_NEXT=<upcoming-commit-sha> REF_NEXT accepts a 40-character commit hash or a vX.Y.Z tag; the strict release check validates it is immutable. The rendered descriptor is written to build/community-extensions/extensions/zarr/description.yml . The community-release.yml workflow exposes the same ref_next as a dispatch input. Practical flow when a new DuckDB line is announced: Branch off main , apply the migration (CI-tools codename branch, version pins, any source fixes), and get CI green — this is the commit tracked by the duckdb-major-bump issue the drift bot opens. Submit a community PR whose descriptor sets ref to the current stable release and ref_next to that branch's HEAD commit. Once DuckDB releases, promote ref_next to ref on your next routine submission.
