docs.text: duckdb-zarr is a DuckDB extension that reads Zarr stores as SQL tables. You point a query at a Zarr store on disk or at a URL, and the arrays inside it come back as rows and columns that you can filter, aggregate and join with any other data DuckDB can read: CSV files, Parquet files, other databases. This document explains the design: how an N-dimensional array becomes a table, which conventions the reader follows, what happens when a query runs, and why the main decisions went the way they did. It describes the extension as it is built today, including its limits, and ends with what is planned. It is written for two groups of readers. If you work with scientific arrays (climate model output, microscopy images, single-cell matrices) and know xarray or NumPy better than SQL, start with Background for array users . If you know SQL and DuckDB but have not met Zarr, start with Background for SQL users . Contributors will find a map of the source code at the end. For task-oriented guides, see Querying AnnData stores and Querying OME-Zarr .
docs.title: How duckdb-zarr works

docs.text: Zarr is a storage format for N-dimensional arrays. An array is a grid of values of one type: a 2-D array of 16-bit integers can hold an image, a 3-D array of floats might hold air temperature over time, latitude and longitude. The number of dimensions (axes) is the array's rank , and the length along each axis is its shape : a temperature array with shape (2920, 25, 53) holds 2,920 time steps on a grid of 25 latitudes by 53 longitudes, 3.9 million values in all. Zarr splits each array into chunks , rectangular blocks of equal shape, and stores each chunk as a separate compressed object: a file on disk, or an object in cloud storage such as Amazon S3. The temperature array above might be chunked (730, 13, 27) , so one chunk covers 730 time steps of one quarter of the grid. A reader that needs only part of an array fetches and decompresses only the chunks that overlap that part. This is why Zarr works well for data far larger than memory, read over a network. The chunks at the far edge of an array can extend past its end; the extra positions hold the array's fill value . A chunk that was never written also reads as the fill value, so a mostly empty array costs little storage. The compression and byte layout of each chunk are described by a list of codecs (gzip, zstd, Blosc, and others) in the array's metadata. A Zarr store is a hierarchy, like a directory tree. Arrays live in groups , and groups can contain other groups. Each array and each group has a small JSON metadata document, and can carry attributes : arbitrary JSON key-value pairs that tools use to record units, descriptions and conventions. There are two versions of the format. Zarr v2 keeps an array's metadata in a .zarray file and its attributes in .zattrs . Zarr v3 keeps both in one zarr.json file. Object stores such as S3 cannot list the contents of a "directory" cheaply, so many published stores also carry consolidated metadata : one document at the root that contains the metadata of every array and group. In v2 this is a .zmetadata file; in v3 it is a block inside the root zarr.json .
docs.title: Zarr, for SQL users

docs.text: Zarr itself only stores arrays. The meaning of their axes comes from conventions layered on top, and the most widespread is xarray 's, a Python library for labelled N-dimensional data. In xarray's model, every axis of an array has a dimension name , such as time , lat or lon . Arrays that share a dimension name share that axis. A coordinate is a 1-D array that labels the positions along a dimension and has the dimension's name: the lat array holds the 25 latitudes of the lat dimension. Most other arrays are data variables : air(time, lat, lon) is a data variable over three dimensions. A collection of data variables and coordinates is an xarray Dataset . A tree of datasets, one per Zarr group, is an xarray DataTree . When xarray writes Zarr, it stores dimension names in the array's _ARRAY_DIMENSIONS attribute (v2) or in the dimension_names field of zarr.json (v3). The CF conventions (Climate and Forecast) are a standard set of attributes from the climate and ocean sciences that xarray and NetCDF tools follow. The ones that matter here: Missing values. A _FillValue or missing_value attribute names a sentinel value (for example -9999 ) that marks a cell as missing. Packing. An integer array with scale_factor and add_offset attributes stores a real-valued measurement compactly. The true value is stored * scale_factor + add_offset . Air temperature stored as the 16-bit integer 27315 with a scale factor of 0.01 is 273.15 kelvin. Time. A time coordinate is often stored as numbers with a units attribute such as "hours since 1900-01-01" and a calendar attribute such as "standard" or "noleap" (a 365-day calendar some climate models use). Bounds. A coordinate can point, through a bounds attribute, to a companion array of shape (N, 2) holding the start and end of each cell, such as time_bnds . Auxiliary coordinates. A data variable's coordinates attribute can name extra coordinate arrays that are not indexed by a single dimension, such as a 2-D lat(y, x) on a curvilinear ocean grid. Two other communities define their own layouts on Zarr, and the extension understands both. OME-Zarr stores microscopy images as a multiscale pyramid : arrays 0 , 1 , 2 , ... hold the same image at decreasing resolution, and the group's multiscales attribute names the axes ( c , z , y , x for channel, depth and the two image axes). AnnData stores annotated matrices, most often single-cell gene expression: a matrix X of observations (cells) by variables (genes), with tables of annotations for each axis.
docs.title: xarray and the CF conventions

docs.text: SQL is the language of relational databases. Its unit of data is the table : a set of rows , each with the same named, typed columns . A query describes the result you want and the database works out how to compute it: SELECT lat, AVG(air) AS mean_air FROM some_table WHERE time >= TIMESTAMP '2014-01-01' GROUP BY lat ORDER BY lat; SELECT picks the output columns, FROM names the input, WHERE keeps the rows that match a condition, and GROUP BY collapses rows that share a value into one row per group, with aggregates such as AVG , SUM and COUNT . A JOIN combines rows of two tables that match on some columns. Rows in a table have no inherent order, so a query that needs one says ORDER BY . A missing value in SQL is NULL . It is not the same as a floating-point NaN : aggregates skip NULL , but a single NaN makes AVG return NaN . DuckDB is a SQL database that runs inside your program (a Python session, a command-line shell, a web page) rather than as a separate server. It is built for analytical queries over large tables, and it reads files in place: FROM 'data.parquet' queries a Parquet file without importing it first. Extensions add features to DuckDB at run time; this project is one. Extensions can add table functions , which are functions that return a table and can appear in FROM like a table. read_zarr('store.zarr') is a table function. Table functions take named parameters , written name := value (DuckDB also accepts name = value ). An extension can also add a replacement scan , which is a hook that turns a string in FROM , such as FROM 'store.zarr' , into a call to one of its functions. A DuckDB database holds schemas , and a schema holds tables and views . A view is a stored query that you can select from like a table. ATTACH adds a database to a session, so era5.main.surface names the view surface in schema main of the attached database era5 . DuckDB processes data in vectors : batches of values for one column, by default up to 2,048 of them. A table function fills one batch of rows per call, and DuckDB can call it from several threads at once.
docs.title: DuckDB and SQL, for array users

docs.text: The extension turns arrays into a table by giving each cell its own row. Each dimension becomes a column holding that cell's coordinate value, and each data variable becomes a column holding that cell's value. Take a store with coordinates time (2 values), lat (2 values) and lon (3 values), and two data variables temperature(time, lat, lon) and humidity(time, lat, lon) . It reads as one table with 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 rows: time lat lon temperature humidity 2024-01-01 00:00 10.0 0.0 273.15 0.81 2024-01-01 00:00 10.0 0.5 273.42 0.79 2024-01-01 00:00 10.0 1.0 273.60 0.78 2024-01-01 00:00 10.5 0.0 272.90 0.83 ... This "long" layout is what lets plain SQL work on gridded data. A spatial average is GROUP BY lat, lon , a time series at a point is WHERE lat = 10.0 AND lon = 0.5 , and joining to a table of weather stations is an ordinary JOIN on lat and lon . It is the same layout as xarray's Dataset.to_dataframe() and the xarray-sql project, which does the same job for the DataFusion query engine. The coordinate columns repeat a lot: each lat value appears once for every combination of time and lon . The extension never builds this table in memory. It generates the rows chunk by chunk as DuckDB asks for them (see How a query runs ), so the cost of a query grows with the chunks it reads, not with the size of the product. A dimension with no coordinate array still gets a column. It holds the position along that axis, 0 to N - 1 , as a BIGINT .
docs.title: One row per cell

docs.text: Variables over different dimensions cannot share rows. A weather reanalysis such as ERA5 has surface variables over (time, latitude, longitude) and atmospheric variables over (time, level, latitude, longitude) , where level is a pressure level. Putting both in one table would repeat each surface value once per level, or fill most of the table with NULL . So a group's data variables are split into tables , one for each set of dimension names (and shape) they share. The test fixture era5_like.zarr reads as two tables: Table Dimensions Columns time_latitude_longitude time, latitude, longitude 10m_u_component_of_wind , 2m_temperature , total_precipitation time_level_latitude_longitude time, level, latitude, longitude geopotential , temperature A table's name is its dimension names joined with underscores, in order. xarray-sql uses the same rule, so both projects give a store the same table names. Two tables in one group whose names differ only in ASCII letter case get no name (DuckDB identifiers ignore case); dims := can still read them. Arrays that are metadata rather than data are kept out of tables: bounds arrays, auxiliary coordinates, and 0-dimensional constants, such as the physical parameters some ocean models store as arrays. (Inside AnnData objects, only the last rule applies, since the CF attributes have no meaning there.) They still appear in read_zarr_metadata .
docs.title: One table per set of dimensions

docs.text: A nested store has one set of tables per group, the way an xarray DataTree has one dataset per node. read_zarr(store) reads the root group, like xarray.open_zarr(store) ; group_path := selects another group, like xarray's group= argument. Arrays in different groups never share a table, even if their names and dimensions match, because sibling groups often reuse dimension names with different lengths: the levels of a simulation at two resolutions, or the members of an ensemble. A group can use the coordinates of its ancestors. If the root has an x coordinate and simulation/fine has foo(x, y) but no x array, the simulation/fine table takes its x column from the root. As in xarray, a group whose dimension lengths disagree with its parent's is misaligned , and its tables cannot be read as tables (single arrays in it still can, through array_path := ). When a store is mounted as a DuckDB database (see Giving tables names ), each group becomes a schema: the root is main , and a nested group is a schema named by its path, quoted because it contains a slash: sim."simulation/fine".x_y .
docs.title: Groups become schemas

docs.text: Some writers record no dimension names. Plain zarr-python does not, and neither does AnnData. Such arrays are left out of tables. The extension does not guess, because a guess could be silently wrong: if every unnamed 1-D array of length 500 got the dimension name dim_0 , two unrelated arrays would end up in one table, joined row by row, with no error. You can still read one such array by its path with array_path := . Its axes are then named dim_0 , dim_1 , and so on, which is safe because only one array is involved. If a group has no other data, read_zarr fails with an error that names the unnamed arrays and suggests array_path := . Pass dims := alongside array_path := to replace those placeholder names with your own, one non-empty, non-NULL name per axis, distinct ignoring case: SELECT sample, good FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/unsupported_dtype.zarr', array_path := 'good', dims := ['sample']) ORDER BY sample; The names still label integer positions; they do not bind sibling coordinate arrays or modify the store. Omitting dims := keeps dim_0 , dim_1 , and so on. An array that already has axis names still requires dims := to match those names exactly — it cannot relabel them. If a value column's name or its value alias then conflicts with a supplied axis name, it gets a numbered suffix such as plain_1 or value_1 , leaving the axis name unchanged. An array that names some of its axes but leaves others empty (a null entry in dimension_names ) is treated differently: the empty entries become dim_<position> even in table reads, so two such arrays can end up sharing a dim_0 axis. See Known limits . Two layouts supply names that the arrays themselves lack. In OME-Zarr, an array takes its axis names from its group's multiscales attribute, so a microscopy image reads with c , z , y , x columns. The levels of a pyramid share those names but not their shapes, so each level is read on its own with array_path := . For AnnData, the extension names each axis from the element's place in the AnnData object, described next.
docs.title: Arrays without dimension names

docs.text: An AnnData object is a group with the attribute encoding-type: anndata . It may be the root of a store written by AnnData.write_zarr() , a table inside a SpatialData store ( tables/<name> ), or a modality of a MuData store ( mod/<name> ). Inside one, the extension applies three extra rules on top of the general model. First, it names the axes. The observation axis is obs and the variable axis is var , so X , the main matrix, has dimensions (obs, var) . AnnData keeps the annotations of each axis in a data frame, also named obs and var . Their columns are read as tables of the AnnData group itself, beside X , so the root of an AnnData store has the tables obs , var and obs_var . Each data frame's index (cell or gene names) becomes the coordinate of its axis, so every table can be filtered and joined by name: WHERE obs = 'AAACATACAACCAC-1' AND var = 'MKI67' . Second, it decodes AnnData's encoded columns. AnnData stores some columns as a group of arrays. A categorical column is integer codes plus a list of categories, and reads as a DuckDB ENUM (or as the categories' own type, when they are not distinct strings). A nullable column is values plus a mask, and reads with NULL where the mask is set. Third, it reads sparse matrices as their stored entries. A sparse matrix ( csr_matrix or csc_matrix ) stores only its nonzero entries. A table that holds only sparse matrices has one row per stored entry, not one row per cell: expanding a 2,700 × 32,738 matrix with 2.3 million stored values would produce 88 million rows. Queries that average over cells must account for the zeros a sparse table omits. The AnnData guide has the full mapping of elements to tables and examples of these queries.
docs.title: AnnData stores

docs.text: read_zarr(store) reads one table. The store is a local path or a URL. SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/float_baseline.zarr'); If the group being read has tables over more than one set of dimensions, read_zarr needs to know which one. Otherwise it fails with an error such as group '/' has 2 tables [...]; use table_name= or dims= to select one, or array_path= to read one array . Parameter Meaning table_name := 'time_lat_lon' Read the table with this name, as read_zarr_tables lists it. Letter case is ignored. Alias "table" . dims := ['time', 'lat', 'lon'] Read the table with these dimension names, in this order. An alternative to table_name ; do not pass both. group_path := 'simulation/fine' Read from this group instead of the root. Slashes at either end are optional. Alias "group" . array_path := 'labels/nuclei/0' Read one array by its path in the store. Its dimensions are its own, an OME-Zarr image's axes, AnnData's axis names, or dim_0 , dim_1 , .... Alias "array" . Cannot be combined with group_path or table_name . bounds := [['lat', '-30', '30'], ...] Read only coordinate ranges. A workaround until WHERE is pushed down; see Selecting coordinate ranges . decode_times := false Leave CF time coordinates as their stored numbers instead of TIMESTAMP . The default is true , as in xarray.open_zarr . The aliases "table" , "group" and "array" need double quotes because TABLE , GROUP and ARRAY are SQL keywords. The columns of a table are its dimensions, in order, then its data variables. In a table read, a column is named after the variable within its group ( foo ), not its path in the store ( simulation/fine/foo ); with array_path := , the path is the name. When the only data column's name would be a number or a path, as with an OME-Zarr resolution level 0 , it is named value instead, so you do not have to quote it: SELECT c, AVG(value) AS mean_intensity FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr', array_path := '0') GROUP BY c;
docs.title: read_zarr

docs.text: A string ending in .zarr in FROM is read with read_zarr : SELECT lat, lon, AVG(temperature) FROM 'test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/float_baseline.zarr' GROUP BY lat, lon; The check ignores letter case and a trailing slash, so s3://bucket/store.zarr/ works too. For a local path, the extension also checks that a zarr.json or .zgroup file exists at that path, so that a directory merely named .zarr falls through to DuckDB's other readers. For URLs ( http:// , https:// , s3:// , gs:// , az:// ) the suffix alone decides, because checking would cost a network request. Paths without the .zarr suffix are never claimed; read them with read_zarr(path) . This form takes no parameters, so it only works when the store's root group has a single table.
docs.title: Querying a path directly

docs.text: Two table functions describe a store without reading any chunk data. read_zarr_metadata(store) lists every array, one row each: Column Type Meaning name VARCHAR Path of the array in the store dims VARCHAR[] Declared dimension names (empty if none) dtype VARCHAR Zarr data type shape , chunk_shape UBIGINT[] Array shape and chunk shape attrs VARCHAR Attributes, as JSON text role VARCHAR coord , data , aux_coord , bounds , scalar or unsupported array_path_dims VARCHAR[] The dimension names read_zarr(store, array_path := name) would use An array that the underlying Zarr library cannot open, for example because of an unsupported data type or codec, is listed with role and dtype unsupported and the error text in attrs , instead of failing the call. read_zarr_tables(store) lists every table in every group, one row each: Column Type Meaning group_path VARCHAR The group, as a path ( / , /simulation/fine ) schema_name VARCHAR The schema the group mounts as ( main for the root) table_name VARCHAR The table's name, or NULL if it cannot be read as one table dims VARCHAR[] Dimension names shape UBIGINT[] Length of each dimension chunk_shape UBIGINT[] The chunk grid the scan uses (see Mixed chunk shapes ) data_vars , coord_vars VARCHAR[] Paths of the arrays (or AnnData encoded groups) that supply its columns The list columns can be searched with DuckDB's list functions: SELECT table_name FROM read_zarr_tables('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/era5_like.zarr') WHERE list_contains(data_vars, 'temperature'); A NULL table_name means the row is listed for inspection but read_zarr cannot read it by name: its group is misaligned, it shares dimension names with an array of a different shape (as the levels of an OME-Zarr pyramid do), it contains an array that cannot be opened, it mixes CSR and CSC sparse matrices, or its name collides with another table's after case folding. Only the last case can be read with dims := ; for the others, read arrays one at a time with array_path := . Both functions accept group_path := and array_path := to narrow the listing. read_zarr_groups is the older name of read_zarr_tables and still works.
docs.title: Inspecting a store

docs.text: For repeated queries it is convenient to give each table a short, stable name. xarray-sql does this in one call, ctx.from_dataset('era5', ds, table_names=...) , after which era5.surface is a table. The design we want for this extension is the same: one call that registers a store under a name, then plain table names in queries. It is planned for DuckDB 2.0 (see A named store, the planned design below). The C API the extension uses today cannot do it, because it gives an extension no way to create views or schemas on the caller's connection. Until then there are two workarounds.
docs.title: Giving tables names

docs.text: A view is one line per table: CREATE VIEW surface AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/era5_like.zarr', table_name := 'time_latitude_longitude'); SELECT AVG("2m_temperature") FROM surface; For a nested group, create a schema for it first, or pick any name you like. The view stores no data; it calls read_zarr each time it is queried. In a database file, views persist across sessions.
docs.title: Workaround: create the views yourself

docs.text: For a store with many tables, read_zarr_views(store, database) writes those statements for you. It does not run them. Like the other functions here, it returns a table, and each row holds one SQL statement as text, in a column named sql : Column Type Meaning schema_name VARCHAR The schema the statement creates or adds to ( NULL for the ATTACH ) view_name VARCHAR The view the statement creates ( NULL for ATTACH and CREATE SCHEMA ) sql VARCHAR The statement Run the statements in order and the store is mounted as a DuckDB database: one ATTACH of an in-memory database, one CREATE SCHEMA per nested group that has a named table, and one CREATE VIEW per named table. The query below selects just the sql column; the comments show the rows it returns: SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/era5_like.zarr', 'era5', view_names := MAP {'time_latitude_longitude': 'surface', 'time_level_latitude_longitude': 'atmosphere'}); -- ATTACH ':memory:' AS "era5"; -- CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "era5"."main"."surface" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('...', table_name := 'time_latitude_longitude'); -- CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW "era5"."main"."atmosphere" AS SELECT * FROM read_zarr('...', table_name := 'time_level_latitude_longitude'); view_names renames views, like xarray-sql's table_names . Its keys are table names for tables in the root group and group/path/table_name for the others. A key that names no table, or a rename that gives two views in one schema the same name, is an error. Tables with a NULL table_name get no view. The ATTACH fails if the database name is already in use; detach the old mount first or pick another name. From Python, run each returned row: mount = """ SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/era5_like.zarr', 'era5', view_names := MAP {'time_level_latitude_longitude': 'atmosphere'}) """ for (sql,) in con.sql(mount).fetchall(): con.execute(sql) In the DuckDB command-line shell, write the rows to a file and read it back: .bail on .mode list .headers off .once mount.sql SELECT sql FROM read_zarr_views('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/era5_like.zarr', 'era5', view_names := MAP {'time_level_latitude_longitude': 'atmosphere'}); .read mount.sql After mounting, SELECT level, AVG(temperature) FROM era5.atmosphere GROUP BY level works like a query on any other table. Without view_names , the same view is era5.main.time_level_latitude_longitude .
docs.title: Workaround: generate the views with read_zarr_views

docs.text: Not built yet. On DuckDB 2.0's v2 C API, mounting becomes one call and needs no generated SQL: SELECT * FROM zarr_mount('era5.zarr', 'era5', table_names := MAP {'time_latitude_longitude': 'surface'}); SELECT AVG("2m_temperature") FROM era5.surface; zarr_mount records the name era5 , the store, and its table names in the extension's memory, and returns the tables it registered. Nothing is added to DuckDB's catalog. When a query names era5.surface , DuckDB does not find it in the catalog and offers the name to the extension's replacement scan (see Querying a path directly ), which turns it into read_zarr('era5.zarr', table_name := 'time_latitude_longitude') . Nested groups work the same way: era5."simulation/fine".x_y . DuckDB 2.0.0 already routes such names to replacement scans. In a test with the current extension, a reference DuckDB could not find in its catalog reached the replacement scan whether it was qualified by a schema or database that did not exist, by an attached database or existing schema of the same name, by three parts, or by a quoted nested schema, and it did so from a second connection to the same database too. A real view with the same name took precedence. What the design needs from the v2 API is the full name. Its replacement scan receives the whole table reference ( era5.surface ), where the v1 API passes only the last part ( surface ), which cannot tell two mounted stores apart. The port to the v2 API is planned anyway for filter pushdown. The design has costs of its own. Mounted tables do not appear in SHOW TABLES , information_schema or autocompletion, so a zarr_mounts() function would list them. A real table or view with the same name takes precedence, because DuckDB tries replacement scans only when its lookup fails. Mounts would be shared by every connection to the database and last as long as it is open, not across sessions; views in a database file remain the way to persist names.
docs.title: A named store, the planned design

docs.text: bounds := is a workaround. The C API the extension is built on gives a table function no access to a query's WHERE conditions, so a WHERE clause on a coordinate column gives the right answer without making the read smaller: the extension reads every chunk and DuckDB discards the rows that do not match (see Filters and pruning ). Until the extension moves to an API with filter pushdown (see Roadmap ), pass the ranges to read_zarr with bounds := to read less. Once pushdown ships, the same WHERE clause will skip the same chunks, and bounds := will not be needed. SELECT time, lat, lon, value FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/bounds_grid.zarr', bounds := [['time', '2020-01-01 02:00:00', '2020-01-01 02:00:00'], ['lat', '-30', '30']]); Each entry is [dimension, low, high] . Both ends are inclusive and written as strings, because a SQL list cannot mix a dimension name with numbers. NULL leaves an end open. Times are written YYYY-MM-DD , optionally followed by HH:MM , seconds and fractional seconds. The scan skips every chunk that holds no coordinate in range, then drops the rows outside the range from the chunks it does read, so the result is exact. Some ranges are refused rather than answered approximately. A dimension needs a stored numeric or time coordinate: positional 0..N-1 columns and string labels (such as AnnData cell names) cannot be bounded, so filter those with WHERE . Ranges compare values as 64-bit floats, so for integer and time coordinates a range is rejected if an endpoint or any coordinate value has a magnitude of 2^53 or more, which a float cannot represent exactly. DuckDB counts timestamps in microseconds since 1970, so this rules out time axes that reach before about 1685 or after about 2255. With decode_times := false , time ranges use the raw stored numbers. Tables made only of sparse matrices are filtered row by row but not pruned by chunk.
docs.title: Selecting coordinate ranges

docs.text: DuckDB runs a table function in three phases: bind , once per query, decides the output columns; init prepares the scan; the scan function is then called repeatedly, each call filling one batch of rows, until it returns an empty batch.
docs.title: How a query runs

docs.text: Open the store. Pick a storage backend from the path (see Where stores can live ). List the arrays. For a local store, walk the directory tree, looking for zarr.json (v3) or .zarray (v2). For a remote store, read the list from consolidated metadata, since object stores cannot list directories cheaply. Build the tree of tables. For each group, read each array's dimension names from dimension_names (v3) or _ARRAY_DIMENSIONS (v2), then from OME-Zarr or AnnData layouts where those apply. Set aside bounds arrays, auxiliary coordinates, 0-dimensional arrays and arrays without names. Identify coordinates: a 1-D array whose only dimension has its own name. Group the remaining arrays by dimension names and shape, resolve each dimension's coordinate from the group or its nearest ancestor, and check alignment with the parent group. Choose one table from table_name , dims , array_path , or the only table in the group. Load the coordinates. Each coordinate array is read whole into memory. Coordinates are 1-D and small next to the data (ERA5's latitude, longitude and time axes together fit in a few megabytes). Decide each column's type and decoding. Each column gets a DuckDB type and a decoding rule: plain, packed integer, CF time, or AnnData categorical, plus a missing-value sentinel (see Reading values correctly ).
docs.title: Bind: from a path to a schema

docs.text: The scan is divided into work units , one per cell of the table's chunk grid. If the table's chunks are 24 × 10 × 10 over (time, lat, lon) , there is one work unit for every block of 24 time steps, 10 latitudes and 10 longitudes, and the work units are listed in row-major order (the last dimension varies fastest). With bounds := , work units with no coordinate in range are dropped here, before any data is read.
docs.title: Plan: work units

docs.text: Each call to the scan function takes the current work unit, decodes the chunk of each data variable the query uses, and writes rows until the batch is full or the chunk runs out. Then it moves to the next work unit. Writing rows from a decoded chunk is the core of the extension. A chunk of shape (s₀, s₁, …, s_{D-1}) holds s₀ × s₁ × … × s_{D-1} cells, stored in row-major order. The scan walks them with a flat row counter i and recovers each cell's position along every dimension with the row-major strides: stride[k] = s[k+1] × s[k+2] × … × s[D-1] (stride[D-1] = 1) index[k] = (i / stride[k]) mod s[k] (integer division) For a chunk of shape (2, 3) , rows 0 to 5 have positions (0,0) (0,1) (0,2) (1,0) (1,1) (1,2) . Each data column reads the cell at those positions from its decoded chunk. Each coordinate column looks up its coordinate array at the chunk's starting offset plus index[k] . The coordinate columns are never stored repeated; they are produced from the 1-D arrays as each batch is written. The batch size is read from DuckDB at run time rather than assumed to be 2,048. The chunks at the far edge of an array can be cut short by the array's end. The Zarr library still returns the chunk at its full size, padded with fill values. The scan then uses two sets of strides: those of the clipped shape, inside the array, to enumerate rows, and those of the full chunk shape to find each cell in the buffer. Data variables the query does not mention are not decoded. SELECT time, lat, lon, temperature on a table that also has humidity never reads a humidity chunk. Coordinates are loaded at bind regardless.
docs.title: Scan: from a chunk to rows

docs.text: Variables in one table do not always share a chunk shape. In the air_temperature_gradient dataset from the xarray tutorial, Tair is chunked (730, 13, 27) and dTdx (730, 7, 27) , because they came from NetCDF variables stored differently. AnnData tables hit the same problem, since zarr-python picks each array's chunks from its data type: in a store of 500,000 cells, an int8 column might be chunked (250000,) and a float64 column (62500,) . The work-unit grid is therefore the largest chunk length in each dimension over the table's dense arrays; read_zarr_tables shows it as chunk_shape . An array chunked like the grid reads one chunk per work unit. Any other array reads the work unit's region as a subset, which decodes each of its chunks the region touches. When the smaller chunks fit evenly inside the grid, as power-of-two chunk sizes do, each is decoded once. When they do not (7 against 13), a chunk that straddles two work units is decoded twice.
docs.title: Mixed chunk shapes

docs.text: A table made only of sparse matrices has a different plan: it produces one row per stored entry, by walking the matrix's compressed row (CSR) or column (CSC) structure, rather than one row per cell. When a table has several sparse matrices, the rows are the union of their stored positions, with 0 for a matrix that has nothing at a position another one stores. A sparse matrix in a table that also has a dense array is read densely, one row per cell, because the dense array needs every row anyway.
docs.title: Sparse tables

docs.text: Pruning means skipping chunks that cannot contribute to the result. It matters: in one measurement, a one-day slice of the ARCO-ERA5 store needed 3 of its 69,033 chunks. Today the scan does not see a query's WHERE conditions. DuckDB applies them to the rows the scan returns, so results are correct, but the scan reads every chunk of the table. The bounds := parameter is the explicit substitute. The reason is the interface the extension is built on. DuckDB's own readers, such as its Parquet reader, receive WHERE conditions through DuckDB's C++ interface. Extensions written in Rust use DuckDB's C API instead, and the extension currently uses version 1.5.6 of it, which has no such hook, so that one binary loads in both DuckDB 1.5.6 and 2.0. DuckDB 2.0 adds a second C API, the v2 API, which does have one: during optimization, the scan is offered each WHERE condition and can accept the ones it will apply itself; DuckDB keeps applying the rest. Moving to it is the planned route to pushdown (see Roadmap ). The range logic behind bounds := is kept separate from the parameter so that pushed conditions can reuse it. Projection pushdown, telling the scan which columns a query uses, works in both C APIs, and the extension uses it as described above.
docs.title: Filters and pruning

docs.text: The extension asks DuckDB for as many threads as there are work units, and threads take work units from a shared counter. In the current version, all threads also share one lock that is held while a chunk is decoded, so in practice chunks are decoded one at a time. See Known limits .
docs.title: Threads

docs.text: Zarr data type DuckDB type bool BOOLEAN int8 , int16 , int32 , int64 TINYINT , SMALLINT , INTEGER , BIGINT uint8 , uint16 , uint32 , uint64 UTINYINT , USMALLINT , UINTEGER , UBIGINT float32 , float64 FLOAT , DOUBLE string (v3), or \|O with the vlen-utf8 filter (v2) VARCHAR any integer type with CF packing attributes DOUBLE any numeric type with CF time attributes TIMESTAMP AnnData categorical of distinct strings ENUM Other types are not supported yet, including NumPy datetime64 , fixed-width byte and Unicode strings, complex numbers and structured types. If the Zarr library can open the array, read_zarr fails at bind with unsupported dtype ; if it cannot, the array is listed as unsupported (see Inspecting a store ). Arrays can be little- or big-endian on disk; the Zarr library converts them to the machine's byte order when it decodes a chunk. The codecs available are those of the zarrs library this extension builds on: gzip, zstd, Blosc (on all platforms except Windows with the GNU toolchain), CRC32C checksums, sharding and transpose.
docs.title: Data types

docs.text: A cell becomes SQL NULL when its stored value equals the variable's missing-value sentinel. The sentinel is chosen once per variable: The _FillValue attribute, if present and readable as the array's type. If it is NaN and a missing_value attribute also exists, missing_value is used instead, because xarray writes _FillValue = NaN for data whose real sentinel it has already replaced in memory. Otherwise the missing_value attribute. Otherwise the array's Zarr fill_value , unless all its bytes are zero (so 0 and 0.0 are not sentinels). Boolean and string fill values are never used. A NaN sentinel matches any NaN , since NaN never equals itself. Without a NaN sentinel, a NaN in a float column stays NaN , not NULL . String columns are never masked, and AnnData's encoded columns use their own masks instead. xarray writes a floating-point _FillValue in Zarr v3 as a base64 string of the value's 8 little-endian bytes ( NaN is "AAAAAAAA+H8=" ). The extension decodes these. Rule 3 means that, in an array without CF attributes, a real value equal to a nonzero fill_value also reads as NULL . See Known limits .
docs.title: Missing values

docs.text: A variable is packed when its stored type is an integer and it has a scale_factor or add_offset attribute (a missing one defaults to 1 or 0). Its column is DOUBLE , and each cell is computed as stored × scale_factor + add_offset . The comparison against the missing-value sentinel happens before scaling, as CF requires: the sentinel is a stored integer, and scaling it first would change it. The integer requirement matters. Some float arrays carry a scale_factor attribute as leftover metadata, and scaling values that are already real numbers would corrupt them.
docs.title: Packed integers

docs.text: A coordinate or variable whose units attribute reads "<unit> since <reference date>" is a CF time axis. The extension converts it to TIMESTAMP , so time conditions read naturally: SELECT date_trunc('month', time) AS month, AVG(air) AS mean_air FROM 'test/fixtures/xarray_tutorial/air_temperature.zarr' WHERE time >= TIMESTAMP '2014-01-01' GROUP BY month ORDER BY month; Without the conversion, ERA5's time would read as a count of hours since 1900, and every query would need to look up that attribute to write TIMESTAMP '1900-01-01' + INTERVAL (time) HOUR . Only calendars that match the real-world calendar are converted: proleptic_gregorian , and standard or gregorian (the default when no calendar is given) from 15 October 1582, when the Gregorian calendar began. Dates before then in a standard axis follow the older Julian calendar in the file's own terms. If the reference date is that early, the axis keeps its stored numbers; if only some values are, those values read as NULL rather than as dates about ten days off. Model calendars such as noleap , all_leap , 360_day and julian have dates that a real calendar lacks, such as 30 February, so those axes keep their stored numbers. Their units and calendar attributes are visible in read_zarr_metadata . Some details of the conversion: Units can be weeks , days , hours , minutes , seconds , milliseconds , microseconds or nanoseconds , with the usual abbreviations. months and years are refused, as xarray refuses them, because they have no fixed length. Bare m means metres in the UDUNITS library that defines these names, so it is refused too. Reference dates can be written 1900-01-01 , 1800-01-01 00:00:00 , 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z or 0001-1-1 0:0:0 , with an optional time-zone offset. The offset's sign is optional, because UDUNITS writes a zero offset as 0:00 . Integer offsets are converted with integer arithmetic, and floating-point offsets are split into whole and fractional parts before scaling. The fractional part matters at scale: days since 1800-01-01 reaches about 7 × 10^15 microseconds, beyond the range where a single float multiply is exact to the microsecond. A missing-value sentinel is checked against the stored number before conversion. NaN , and values that would fall outside DuckDB's timestamp range, become NULL . decode_times := false turns the conversion off for the whole query. When an integer variable has both packing attributes and time units, it is decoded as packed; no store in practice packs its time axis. A float variable with both is decoded as time, and its scale_factor is ignored.
docs.title: CF time

docs.text: Variable-length UTF-8 strings, as AnnData and zarr-python write for text columns such as gene symbols, read as VARCHAR . zarrs reads both the v3 string type and the v2 vlen-utf8 encoding.
docs.title: Strings

docs.text: Path How it is read Local path Directly from the file system http:// , https:// With the zarrs HTTP client s3:// , gs:// , az:// Through DuckDB's own file system, so credentials come from DuckDB's secrets manager ( CREATE SECRET ... TYPE S3 ) Routing cloud storage through DuckDB means the extension inherits DuckDB's credentials, retries and configuration instead of reimplementing them. The DuckDB file system is obtained from the query's client context during bind. A remote store needs consolidated metadata to be listed. Most published datasets have it; xarray writes it with to_zarr(..., consolidated=True) . The extension reads it once per query and answers every later metadata lookup from memory, so opening a store with a hundred arrays costs a few requests rather than hundreds. Without consolidated metadata, a remote store can still be read one array at a time with array_path := . This is the usual case for public OME-Zarr images. The extension also builds for WebAssembly and loads in DuckDB-Wasm , which runs DuckDB in a web browser. There, every path, HTTP included, goes through DuckDB's file system, and the Zarr library's internal thread pool runs on a single thread. Local paths do not work in the browser, because listing a local store walks the host's file system.
docs.title: Where stores can live

docs.text: The decisions are numbered so that code comments and tests can refer to them.
docs.title: Design decisions

docs.text: Dimension names come only from metadata: xarray's attribute or field, OME-Zarr's axes, or AnnData's layout. The alternative was to infer roles from shape, so that 1-D arrays are coordinates and the rest are data, as the zarr-datafusion project does. Declared names were chosen because xarray writes most of the stores in this ecosystem and its metadata already gives the right dimension names and order. Shape-based inference was dropped altogether because of the failure described in decision 7.
docs.title: 1. Follow declared dimension names, never guess them

docs.text: The alternatives were one wide table for the whole store, which only works when every variable has the same dimensions, and one table per variable, which makes users join variables they usually want side by side. Grouping by dimensions gives tables with no padding NULL s and keeps related variables in one row. It matches how xarray-sql splits and names tables, so a store gets the same tables in both projects.
docs.title: 2. One table per set of dimensions

docs.text: Converting time to TIMESTAMP is opinionated, and the obvious library for it, the Rust port of cftime, is AGPL-licensed, which rules it out for an extension distributed as a binary. What made it possible was splitting the problem. The calendars that match a wall clock need only ordinary date arithmetic, which the chrono library (already a dependency of DuckDB's Rust crate) provides, and those calendars cover nearly all widely queried data, including ERA5, GPCP and the NCEP reanalyses. The model calendars stay as raw numbers rather than becoming plausible-looking wrong dates. decode_times := false restores the numbers everywhere.
docs.title: 3. Decode CF time, but only on real-world calendars

docs.text: DuckDB offers every string in a FROM clause to each registered replacement scan. Checking the file system for every string would slow down unrelated queries, so the extension considers only strings ending in .zarr , and for local paths confirms with one file check. Other Zarr paths remain reachable through read_zarr(path) .
docs.title: 4. Claim only .zarr paths in FROM

docs.text: zarrs has an asynchronous interface, but DuckDB's table-function callbacks are synchronous, and bridging the two would mean running an async runtime inside each scan. Reads are synchronous. This can be revisited if network latency comes to dominate remote queries.
docs.title: 5. Read synchronously

docs.text: Three options were considered: refuse tables whose variables are chunked differently, plan on the largest chunks and read the other arrays as subsets, or iterate row by row. Refusing was the first implementation, and it turned out to block common data, including NCEP reanalysis stores and the obs table of any large AnnData store. Row-by-row iteration would give up chunked reads. Planning on the largest chunks keeps the scan's structure and lets zarrs do the subset reads, at the cost of decoding some chunks twice when chunk boundaries do not line up (see Mixed chunk shapes ).
docs.title: 6. Mixed chunk shapes share a work-unit grid

docs.text: AnnData and plain zarr-python write no dimension names. Naming such axes dim_0 , dim_1 , ... everywhere would let two unrelated arrays of the same length share dim_0 , land in one table and be joined row by row, returning wrong data with no error. So placeholder names are given only when array_path := selects one array, where nothing can be misaligned, and a placeholder name never matches a coordinate array, even one called dim_0 . Group reads leave unnamed arrays out. Since dims := can replace those placeholder names for one query ( issue #76 ), the same restriction applies: the supplied names only relabel integer positions and never bind sibling coordinates. Arrays that name only some of their axes do not follow this decision yet (see Known limits ). read_zarr_metadata shows both the declared names ( dims ) and the names an array_path read would use ( array_path_dims ), so neither column changes meaning between calls.
docs.title: 7. Give placeholder names only to a single selected array

docs.text: Earlier versions pooled the arrays of every group and grouped them by dimension names alone. That failed with a shape mismatch when two groups reused a dimension name with different lengths, and silently merged them when the lengths agreed. Reading one group at a time, with xarray's rules for inheriting coordinates and checking alignment, is the DataTree model, and following it lets xarray-sql and this extension agree on any store. Store maps to database, group to schema and table to table, the same catalog shape that DataFusion, the engine under xarray-sql, uses. read_zarr_tables publishes that mapping, and it is the whole contract between the two projects. The design we want for naming tables is xarray-sql's: one call registers a store under a name, and its tables are then queried as era5.surface . Three ways to get there were considered: ATTACH 'era5.zarr' AS era5 (TYPE ZARR) , the most natural spelling. Neither DuckDB C API lets an extension add a kind of database to ATTACH , so this is not planned. A procedure that creates the schemas and views. The C API cannot run SQL on the caller's connection, so a prototype ran it through a second connection opened when the extension loaded. That connection kept DuckDB from ever releasing the database, which left database files locked after closing, for every user of the extension. It was rejected. A mount registry with a replacement scan, zarr_mount , described in A named store, the planned design . It creates nothing in DuckDB's catalog, so it needs neither of the missing hooks, only a replacement scan that sees full table names. That arrives with DuckDB 2.0's v2 C API. This is the planned design. Until then, both ways of naming tables are workarounds for the limits of the C API the extension uses today: creating views by hand, and read_zarr_views , which writes the view statements for the user to run.
docs.title: 8. Each group is a node, and a store maps to a database

docs.text: Read as plain Zarr, an AnnData store gives no tables at all (it has no dimension names), integer codes instead of category labels, empty strings instead of NULL for nullable columns, and three unaligned arrays instead of each sparse matrix. Users can decode all of that in SQL, but the queries are long, and two easy mistakes return wrong data without an error. So the extension applies an AnnData layer inside every AnnData group. The main choices: obs and var sit beside X . As groups of their own they would give tables named obs.obs and var.var , and a root with no obs coordinate for X to inherit. Beside X they are what an xarray Dataset of an AnnData object would hold: X(obs, var) , cell_type(obs) , gene_symbol(var) . Names, not positions, label the axes. With each frame's index as the coordinate, every table can be filtered and joined by cell or gene name without a lookup join. Joins then compare strings, and a store with duplicate names gives extra rows; AnnData warns about duplicates and obs_names_make_unique() is a standard step, so the guide documents the risk rather than switching to positions. Embeddings stay long. The second axis of an obsm entry (the components of a PCA or UMAP) has a different length in each entry, so each gets its own dimension, <key>_component . DuckDB array columns were considered and rejected, to keep every value scalar. Sparse matrices read as stored entries. Expanding them to every cell would turn a modest dataset into tens of millions of rows of zeros, and real atlases are a thousand times larger. One row per stored entry is how single-cell users already treat X in SQL. The cost is that averages over cells must add the missing zeros back, for example by starting from the obs table with a LEFT JOIN and averaging COALESCE(X, 0) . Two sparse matrices with the same dimensions must share a table (decision 2), so the table's rows are the union of their entries. Any AnnData group, not just the root. SpatialData keeps its tables as AnnData objects beside OME-Zarr images and Parquet files. Reading those tables needs nothing SpatialData-specific, and DuckDB's read_parquet already reads the rest, so the extension stays a Zarr reader. Not covered yet: awkward-array elements, data frames inside uns , and the global obs and var of a MuData store, which lie outside its AnnData modalities.
docs.title: 9. AnnData: named axes, decoded encodings, stored entries

docs.text: Pushing WHERE conditions into the scan is the goal: it is what users of any database expect, and both xarray-sql and zarr-datafusion do it. The C API the extension uses has no hook for it, so bounds := was added as an explicit stopgap. Its range logic resolves each bound against the coordinate values themselves, so descending axes (ERA5's latitude runs from 90 to -90) and unevenly spaced ones (pressure levels) need no special cases. Ranges are inclusive and checked row by row inside kept chunks. Integer and time values too large for a float to hold exactly are rejected rather than compared approximately. The plan for real pushdown, on DuckDB 2.0's v2 C API, reuses that logic: each accepted condition on a coordinate becomes a set of kept indices, which selects chunks and filters rows exactly as bounds := does. The scan accepts only conditions it can apply exactly (comparisons with a constant, and IN lists), and uses any others only to skip chunks, leaving DuckDB to apply them. That second group includes BETWEEN and other two-sided ranges, which the v2 API passes without saying whether their ends are inclusive ( duckdb/duckdb#25391 , open as of November 2026). With pushdown in place, a WHERE clause does everything bounds := does, so the parameter is no longer needed. It stays for at least one release after pushdown ships, so that existing queries keep working, and is then deprecated.
docs.title: 10. Explicit coordinate ranges until WHERE can be pushed down

docs.text: Reading Zarr (store layout, DataTree and AnnData rules, decoding, CF time, range pruning) lives in a separate crate, zarr-core , whose public types contain no DuckDB or Arrow types. The DuckDB extension is an adapter on top. This keeps the conventions testable on their own and lets other engines reuse them.
docs.title: 11. Keep the Zarr reader independent of DuckDB

docs.text: The Roadmap covers the planned fixes for most of these. No pushdown of WHERE . Every query reads every chunk of its table unless it uses bounds := (see Filters and pruning ). No statistics. The extension reports no row count, so DuckDB's optimizer plans joins on its default guess, and no column statistics. Chunks are decoded one at a time. A lock shared by all scan threads is held during decoding. A nonzero Zarr fill_value reads as NULL in arrays without CF missing-value attributes, even where it is a real value. NaN is not NULL unless the variable's sentinel is NaN . Partly named arrays get placeholder names in table reads. A null entry in dimension_names becomes dim_<position> , so such arrays can share a table, contrary to decision 7. Unsupported data types: NumPy datetime64 , fixed-width strings, complex and structured types. Auxiliary coordinates are dropped. A 2-D lat(y, x) named in a coordinates attribute does not become a column. Model calendars stay numeric. noleap , 360_day , julian and similar time axes are not converted. Coordinates are reloaded for every query, as is consolidated metadata. Remote stores need consolidated metadata, except for single-array reads with array_path := . Local paths do not work in DuckDB-Wasm. A few arrays can drop out of a table without an error: an array with an unsupported data type or codec whose metadata gives no readable shape, and an AnnData encoded column whose values array zarrs cannot open. read_zarr_metadata still lists them. group_path := on a group with no arrays in or below it reports the group as not found. Read-only. The extension does not write Zarr.
docs.title: Known limits

docs.text: The aim is to work like any SQL table and to reach rough parity with xarray-sql and zarr-datafusion . The items below are planned but not built. Each says which DuckDB C API it needs: the v1.5.6 API the extension uses today, or DuckDB 2.0's v2 API. The v2 API changes the plan, so its terms come first. In DuckDB 2.0 every v2 function is marked unstable, so it may change between releases, and an extension built on it is tied to the DuckDB version it was built for. It also does not load in DuckDB 1.5. The duckdb Rust crate for 2.0 (version 1.20000.0 ) includes bindings to it for loadable extensions, but its safe wrapper for table functions still covers only the v1 API, so the port means calling the v2 functions directly.
docs.title: Roadmap

docs.text: Filter pushdown on coordinates (v2 API). Comparisons, IN and ranges on dimension columns select chunks and rows, as decision 10 describes. Pushed conditions could later select index ranges inside a chunk too, as zarr-datafusion does, so that a narrow slice reads less than whole chunks. Row counts for the optimizer (v1 and v2 APIs). DuckDB uses a table's row count to plan joins and choose algorithms. A dense table's count is the product of its shape, known exactly at bind; a sparse table's is the number of stored entries, known after reading the matrices' index arrays. Both sibling projects report exact counts. The extension reports none today. Column statistics (not available in either C API). xarray-sql and zarr-datafusion report exact minimum and maximum values for coordinates, and xarray-sql reports null counts. The extension knows coordinate minima and maxima exactly from the coordinate arrays, but neither DuckDB C API lets a table function report per-column statistics. This needs a change in DuckDB. Parallel scans (v1 and v2 APIs). Both APIs support per-thread scan state, which removes the shared lock described in Threads . On the v2 API the scan can also declare that its rows have no particular order, which lets DuckDB run its output in parallel. Named stores with zarr_mount (v2 API), replacing read_zarr_views and hand-written views as the way to give tables names, as decision 8 and A named store, the planned design describe. Grouped aggregates by coordinate (v2 API). The v2 API lets a scan tell DuckDB that its rows are already partitioned by some columns, so GROUP BY on a coordinate could skip hashing. zarr-datafusion goes further and answers COUNT , MIN and MAX from metadata.
docs.title: Expected of any database

docs.text: NaN as NULL . xarray-sql returns floating-point NaN as NULL , which matches how xarray users treat missing data. The extension keeps NaN unless it is the variable's sentinel. More data types: NumPy datetime64 and timedelta64 , and fixed-width byte and Unicode strings. Both siblings read datetime64 . Dictionary-encoded coordinate columns (v1 API). Coordinate values repeat heavily, and zarr-datafusion encodes them as dictionaries. The v1 API can build dictionary vectors by slicing a vector with a selection vector. Writing Zarr with COPY ... TO 'out.zarr' (v1 API copy functions), as zarr-datafusion supports. A chunks := parameter to set the work-unit size, as xarray-sql's chunks= sets its partitions. Packed float32 output. xarray decodes integers packed with float32 scale factors to float32 ; the extension always uses DOUBLE . Model calendars ( noleap , 360_day , ...). xarray-sql keeps them as numbers and offers a cftime() function for them. Icechunk and virtual Zarr, which zarr-datafusion reads. Icechunk adds Git-like versioning to Zarr; its Rust library is asynchronous only and opens repositories and sessions rather than paths, so it needs an asynchronous storage layer and a way to name snapshots in SQL. Virtual Zarr (Kerchunk and VirtualiZarr manifests) presents existing NetCDF, HDF5 or GRIB2 files as Zarr; their chunks live in other files at offsets given by a manifest, and are often compressed in ways that are not Zarr codecs.
docs.title: Parity with xarray-sql and zarr-datafusion

docs.text: Cache coordinates and consolidated metadata across queries, keyed by store, instead of reloading them in every bind. A configurable chunk cache (a SET option, available in both APIs) is a possible follow-up. Auxiliary coordinates as columns. Neither sibling exposes them (xarray-sql drops them, zarr-datafusion treats them as data), but xarray's own to_dataframe() does. Binding a sibling coordinate array when dims := names an axis of an otherwise unnamed array_path := read ( issue #76 ), so the axis could read real values instead of integer positions. Deferred from the initial dims := naming to keep that change free of any new join-like behavior.
docs.title: Smaller improvements

docs.text: Column statistics, above.
docs.title: Blocked on DuckDB

docs.text: ATTACH 'store.zarr' (TYPE ZARR) . Neither C API lets an extension add a kind of database to ATTACH ; zarr_mount is the planned alternative (decision 8). Substrait, a format for passing query plans between engines. A read_zarr call is specific to DuckDB, so plans that use it cannot run elsewhere; mounted views, which other engines could resolve by name, are a closer fit. variables := and coords := parameters, from an early draft of this design. Selecting columns in SELECT already limits what is decoded, and neither sibling has an override for coordinate roles.
docs.title: Not planned

docs.text: xarray-sql queries xarray datasets with SQL through Apache DataFusion. This extension follows its table layout and naming. zarr-datafusion reads Zarr into DataFusion from Rust. zarrs is the Rust Zarr library this extension uses for metadata, codecs and chunk decoding.

docs.text: Querying OME-Zarr ¶ OME-Zarr images commonly contain several resolution levels and nested label arrays. The examples below run against this repo's small synthetic fixture ( make generate_fixtures first). Start by listing the available arrays: SELECT name, dims, shape, dtype FROM read_zarr_metadata('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr'); The array_path argument is optional. Use it when a store has multiple resolution levels, nested labels, or otherwise ambiguous array groups. The path is the same store-relative path reported by read_zarr_metadata . Then select a resolution level and aggregate by channel: SELECT c, AVG(value) AS mean_intensity FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr', array_path='0') GROUP BY c; Here, 0 is the conventional path for the highest-resolution level. When you select a single array with array_path , its data is exposed as a value column and its xarray dimension names ( c , y , x ) become the other columns — add a WHERE y BETWEEN ... AND x BETWEEN ... clause to aggregate a sub-region. Nested label arrays use the same selector: SELECT value AS label, COUNT(*) AS pixels FROM read_zarr('test/fixtures/bioimage/ome_zarr/synthetic_multichannel.ome.zarr', array_path='labels/nuclei/0') WHERE value > 0 GROUP BY label; Remote OME-Zarr ¶ Public OME-Zarr images can be read straight from a URL. Bioimage stores usually lack consolidated metadata, so whole-store operations ( read_zarr_metadata , or read_zarr without array_path ) aren't available remotely — but a specific resolution level reads by array_path , with c / z / y / x recovered from the OME multiscales.axes : -- A public image from the Image Data Resource (IDR) SELECT c, z, y, x, value AS intensity FROM read_zarr( 'https://uk1s3.embassy.ebi.ac.uk/idr/zarr/v0.4/idr0062A/6001240.zarr', array_path='0' ) LIMIT 10; Filters and aggregates over a full pyramid level scan every chunk (there is no sub-chunk filter pushdown yet), so keep remote exploratory queries bounded with LIMIT or use a coarse resolution level. The duckdb-zarr for biologists browser example queries this original remote image at its full-resolution level 0 , with both channels displayed together in a rotating VTK.js volume. To avoid hundreds of serial chunk requests, the browser fetches the unchanged compressed objects in parallel and registers their original HTTPS URLs in DuckDB-Wasm memory. No prepared dataset or proxy is served by the site. The original Blosc/LZ4 codec works in the tested WASM build; long unprefetched reads were transport latency, not evidence of a codec hang.

docs.text: Versioning ¶ duckdb-zarr follows a dynamic versioning model: the git release tag is the source of truth, and the version strings checked into the repository are development placeholders that get synced from the tag at release time. This mirrors the approach used by the sibling arrow-lint and zarr-lint projects. Two independent version concepts ¶ This project has two version numbers that are easy to conflate: The DuckDB extension's own extension_version metadata — stamped into the compiled .duckdb_extension binary and reported by DuckDB at runtime. The Cargo.toml / pyproject.toml / description.yml version trio — used for the community-extension descriptor and human-facing docs. They are synced independently, by two different mechanisms. The extension's runtime version already reads the git tag ¶ DuckDB's own build tooling ( extension-ci-tools/scripts/configure_helper.py , vendored as a submodule) autodetects the extension version from git and writes it to configure/extension_version.txt : git_tag = subprocess.getoutput("git tag --points-at HEAD") EXTENSION_VERSION = git_tag or subprocess.getoutput("git --no-pager log -1 --format=%h") The Makefile stamps that file's contents into the compiled binary's metadata ( -evf configure/extension_version.txt ). This already works today, with no code in this repository involved — every build, including the one duckdb/community-extensions performs against this repo's tagged ref , is tied to the git tag automatically: LOAD zarr; SELECT extension_version FROM duckdb_extensions() WHERE extension_name = 'zarr'; configure/ is gitignored and rebuilt by make configure , so there is nothing to keep in sync by hand here — this is why the extension itself never needed a Rust source change to "read the git tag": duckdb_extensions() is the read path, and zarrs /the crate's own Cargo.toml version field never enters the picture. (This differs from a typical cargo install able binary, where env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION") really would end up in the shipped artifact — it does not here, because the extension is loaded via DuckDB's C API, not run as a standalone binary carrying its own --version .) Source of truth for the descriptor/docs trio ¶ The Cargo, Python, and community-descriptor version fields are a separate, purely cosmetic concern: they must agree with each other so the rendered description.yml submitted to duckdb/community-extensions and the generated docs are consistent. The committed values are development placeholders — not expected to track the latest release: # Cargo.toml [package] version = "0.1.3" # pyproject.toml [project] version = "0.1.3" # description.yml extension: version: 0.1.3 Verifying consistency ¶ scripts/check_release_ready.py runs on every PR ( Release metadata consistency job in .github/workflows/rust-quality.yml ) and fails if these three placeholders drift apart from each other. It does not check them against any git tag — that's not the release gate, since the placeholder is never expected to already equal the next tag. Release tags ¶ Release tags use a v prefix; the package version omits it: Git tag Package version v0.1.4 0.1.4 At release time, scripts/sync_release_version.py rewrites Cargo.toml , pyproject.toml , description.yml , and the zarr package entry in Cargo.lock to match the tag, inside the release workflow's CI checkout — no commit is made to main (or any branch) : $ python3 scripts/sync_release_version.py v0.1.4 tag=v0.1.4 version=0.1.4: synced Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, description.yml, Cargo.lock $ python3 scripts/sync_release_version.py v0.1.4 --check OK: tag v0.1.4 matches all version sites. This is an ephemeral edit : it only runs inside .github/workflows/community-release.yml 's CI checkout, right before rendering the community descriptor, and is never committed. The repository keeps its development-placeholder version between releases — publishing a release no longer requires a manual Cargo.toml / pyproject.toml / description.yml bump beforehand, only a CHANGELOG.md entry (still maintained by hand; see CHANGELOG.md ) and the tag itself. Committing the synced version back to main was considered and rejected: it would require the release workflow to push a commit (or open a PR) after every tag, adding a second source of truth that could drift from the tag it was derived from, plus bot-authored commits/PRs to review on every release. Leaving the sync ephemeral keeps the git tag as the single source of truth and matches the pattern already proven in arrow-lint / zarr-lint . If a workflow_dispatch run targets a raw commit hash instead of a tag (the description.yml repo.ref "publish an older/manual ref" path), there is no tag to sync from, so the sync step is skipped and the checked-in placeholder is rendered as-is — the same behavior this workflow had before dynamic versioning existed. Why not release-plz? ¶ release-plz automates conventional-commit-driven version bumps, changelog generation, and crates.io publishing via release PRs. It was considered for this issue but doesn't fit duckdb-zarr : this crate is never published to crates.io (it's a cdylib C API extension, not a library), its DuckDB engine test pin and C API compatibility floor are managed separately (see docs/community-extension-release.md ), and the three-file descriptor trio it would still need a custom step for is exactly what sync_release_version.py already handles. The placeholder-plus-tag-sync pattern from arrow-lint / zarr-lint covers the same need with less new surface area and matches the pattern already proven in this maintainer's other projects.

docs.text: Documentation website ¶ The website publishes the existing Markdown guides and the browser biology examples as one static site. The guide content does not need to be rewritten or maintained in a second format. Structure ¶ / — the documentation overview, rendered from docs/README.md . /anndata/ and /ome-zarr/ — the existing biology guides. /examples/climate/ and /examples/geoscience/ — the Markdown field guides. There is no separate field-guide index page; use the direct sidebar links. /biology/ — the first example page: interactive single-cell and 3D images. Its existing URL stays unchanged. The remaining guides stay in the sidebar, with search and section navigation. The documentation and examples share the green-and-cream palette, serif headings, wordmark, and top links: Documentation and GitHub. The published biology page also uses the same sidebar, search, and mobile Browse guides menu, with Biology marked as the active example. The examples also link directly to their corresponding format guides. Links remain relative, including when GitHub Pages hosts the whole site below a project prefix such as /duckdb-zarr/ . Build and preview ¶ Install the biology app's JS dependencies and obtain its matching WASM extension using the biology setup instructions . Then, from the repository root: uv run scripts/build_docs.py python3 -m http.server 4178 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory site Open http://127.0.0.1:4178/ for the docs, then choose Biology under the sidebar's Field guides heading. Use a different port if another preview is already listening on 4178. The build script carries a pinned MkDocs dependency, invokes the existing Vite build, and combines everything under ignored site/ . It stages files only temporarily; it does not edit the source Markdown. It does not download or bundle scientific datasets. The biology app still fetches its original remote sources only when someone opens the interactive page. For biology, the builder stages biology/index.md using the compiled app's main content and asset links. Its biology.html template extends the shared main.html , so navigation comes from mkdocs.yml rather than a copied menu or an iframe. The standalone Vite build remains unchanged. npm run dev inside demos/biology remains useful for editing that app alone. It is not the combined documentation preview, so its parent-documentation links require the combined site above. Updating the site ¶ Edit the existing .md guide files as usual. Change sidebar organization in mkdocs.yml . Change the thin site shell in docs/_theme/ . Set example_title: true in a Markdown example's front matter to use the same title typography and spacing as biology, with a green title-accent span on the second line. Keep demo-only rendering and SQL in demos/biology/ . Add future example pages under docs/examples/ and add direct links to the Field guides section in mkdocs.yml . The section heading is not a link. Separately built interactive apps can keep their own URLs; only those apps need additional build staging. The site-only link hook keeps Markdown links useful in both contexts: links to the demo README become links to the running examples, and links to source or test files outside docs/ go to GitHub. Code examples are left untouched. Deployment and checks ¶ .github/workflows/biology-demo-pages.yml now publishes the entire site/ artifact, not just the demo. Its display name is Documentation Pages . It reuses the checksum-pinned, browser-tested extension artifact from distribution run 40233921996 ; the deploy job does not rebuild the Rust extension. GitHub Pages must use the GitHub Actions build method. The workflow runs for documentation/example changes on main , or by manual dispatch. The pinned artifact must still be available in the same repository; if it expires, deployment fails instead of falling back to an untested binary. The optional run_id input can point to another run, but its artifact must have the pinned name and the digest in demos/biology/extension.sha256 . To adopt a new binary, browser-test it with the pinned DuckDB-Wasm package, then update the workflow's run ID, artifact name and checksum together. CI verifies the checksum and runs helper tests plus a real WASM-reader query against a synthetic format fixture before uploading the Pages artifact. A local build does not publish anything; changes still need to be reviewed and merged before the workflow can deploy them. --skip-demo-build reuses demos/biology/dist and requires both its index.html and zarr.duckdb_extension.wasm . A copy of the extension under public/ cannot repair an incomplete existing build. uv run --no-project --with mkdocs==1.6.1 python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_docsite.py uv run scripts/build_docs.py node demos/biology/test/docsite.browser.mjs site --layout-only node demos/biology/test/docsite.browser.mjs site The --layout-only check verifies identical sidebars, example-title styles, search and mobile menus without starting the biology query engine. It blocks only the app module, preserves its real compiled CSS/HTML, and is not a test of scientific queries or rendering. The full command without that flag still loads and checks the real datasets. The full browser check follows docs → individual field guides → live biology app → docs, exercises search and mobile navigation, checks generated internal links, and loads the real remote data under a GitHub Pages-style project prefix. It uses the existing Playwright installation ( npx playwright install chromium from demos/biology if needed).

docs.text: duckdb-zarr for geoscience. ¶ Explore Landsat surface reflectance and vegetation using SQL over a public Zarr store. These are native DuckDB walkthroughs, not browser-executed cells. Run the SQL blocks in order on the same connection after loading the Zarr extension . The data stay at their original HTTPS source; no local dataset preparation is needed, and no imagery is bundled with this website. Open a small Landsat composite ¶ The New England leaf-on Landsat composites combine cloud-screened Landsat observations into one image per year. Use 2024 and the coarsest pyramid group, leafon/7 , for a small regional overview. Its x and y coordinates are longitude and latitude in EPSG:4326; time contains integer years, not timestamps. This is an annual composite, not an individual Landsat scene. CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW landsat_2024 AS SELECT time AS year, x AS lon, y AS lat, red * 0.0000275 - 0.2 AS red, nir * 0.0000275 - 0.2 AS nir FROM read_zarr( 'https://data.source.coop/kentstephen/landsat-mosaics-new-england/pyramid_v1', group_path := 'leafon/7', bounds := [['time', '2024', '2024']] ) AS pixels WHERE pixels.red BETWEEN 1 AND 65455 AND pixels.nir BETWEEN 1 AND 65455; The bands contain digital numbers. Their documented conversion is reflectance = DN * 0.0000275 - 0.2 ; the store uses scale and offset attributes rather than CF's scale_factor and add_offset , so apply it explicitly. The filter removes nodata zero and values above the published valid range before scaling. Do not compute NDVI directly from these raw numbers: the additive offset does not cancel. Vegetation from Landsat bands ¶ The normalized difference vegetation index is (NIR - red) / (NIR + red) . Each pixel is a row, so the calculation is ordinary column arithmetic: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW landsat_ndvi AS SELECT lon, lat, (nir - red) / NULLIF(nir + red, 0) AS ndvi FROM landsat_2024 WHERE red > 0 AND nir > 0; SELECT lon, lat, ndvi FROM landsat_ndvi ORDER BY lat DESC, lon LIMIT 20; This introductory example keeps positive reflectances; negative reflectance can occur over water or shadow and is not automatically a storage error. NULLIF protects the denominator. Remove LIMIT 20 to return the whole coarse grid for plotting. Higher positive NDVI often indicates vegetation, but NDVI alone is not a land-cover classification. Summarize the vegetation index ¶ SELECT COUNT(*) AS pixels, MIN(ndvi) AS minimum_ndvi, AVG(ndvi) AS mean_ndvi, MAX(ndvi) AS maximum_ndvi, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE ndvi >= 0.5) AS high_ndvi_pixels FROM landsat_ndvi; The threshold is illustrative, not a universal vegetation mask. These coarse bands are averaged before NDVI is calculated: this is not the mean of full-resolution, 30 m pixel NDVI. Use finer levels and appropriate quality masks for a scientific analysis. Data: kentstephen on Source Cooperative, derived from USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Tier 1 surface reflectance via Microsoft Planetary Computer; CC0-1.0. The column-arithmetic example follows the xarray-sql NDVI benchmark , which uses Sentinel-2; the dataset here is Landsat. For temperature and precipitation examples, see the climate guide . The scientific domains page distinguishes the walkthrough from automated fixture coverage. Bring your own questions. duckdb-zarr for the answers. ¶
